tissues.name: Simple squamous epithelium
tissues.summary: Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of thin, flattened cells that lines blood vessels, body cavities, alveoli and the renal capsule. Its very thin, smooth surface allows rapid diffusion and filtration and reduces friction.
features: Flattened cells in a single layer, with the nucleus bulging into the lumen or cavity
Seen from the surface, cells are thin polygons with pale oval nuclei and dark borders
Endothelium lines vessels; mesothelium lines pleura, pericardium and peritoneum
Also forms type I pneumocytes and the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule
Very thin barrier (under 1 µm) allows rapid gas exchange and filtration

tissues.name: Simple cuboidal epithelium
tissues.summary: Simple cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cube-shaped cells, each with a round central nucleus. It lines small ducts and kidney tubules and is specialised for secretion and absorption.
features: Single layer of cube-shaped cells, about as high as they are wide
Round, central nucleus in the middle of each cell
Cells sit on a thin basement membrane with connective tissue beneath
Lumen lined by the cells, as in kidney tubules, thyroid follicles and small gland ducts
Fuzzy brush border (apical microvilli) on proximal tubule cells, facing the lumen

tissues.name: Simple columnar epithelium
tissues.summary: A single layer of tall, column-shaped cells with oval nuclei near their bases, lining the stomach, intestines and gallbladder. The cells absorb nutrients or secrete mucus, and a ciliated form lines the uterine tube.
features: Single layer of tall columnar cells with oval nuclei near the base
Brush border of microvilli on the luminal surface of absorptive cells
Goblet cells, pale and mucus-filled, scattered among the columnar cells of the intestine
Goblet cells are absent from the stomach surface
Ciliated form in the uterine tube, with cilia on the luminal surface

tissues.name: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
tissues.summary: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is a single layer of cells whose nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks layered although every cell touches the basement membrane. It lines the nasal cavity, trachea and bronchi, where cilia and goblet-cell mucus carry trapped particles up towards the pharynx.
features: Nuclei at different heights, though every cell touches the basement membrane
Tall columnar cells with a fringe of motile cilia on the free surface
Goblet cells: pale, mucus-filled cells scattered among the ciliated cells
Basal cells: small round nuclei lying against the basement membrane
Lamina propria below, with blood vessels; cartilage and glands in larger airways

tissues.name: Stratified squamous epithelium (non-keratinised)
tissues.summary: Stratified squamous epithelium without a keratin layer, so its superficial cells stay nucleated. It lines moist surfaces such as the oral cavity, oesophagus, vagina and anal canal, where many cell layers resist abrasion.
features: Many layers of cells with no keratin layer on the surface
Superficial squamous cells are flattened and still have nuclei
Middle layers of polygonal cells that become taller towards the base
Basal layer of cuboidal stem cells on the basement membrane
Glycogen-rich cells in the vagina appear clear
Lines the oral cavity, oesophagus, vagina, ectocervix and anal canal, and covers the cornea

tissues.name: Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinised)
tissues.summary: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium forms the epidermis of the skin. Basal cells divide and move upwards, flattening into anucleate, keratin-filled squames that are shed from the surface and make the skin waterproof.
features: Stratum basale: a single row of cuboidal to columnar cells on the basement membrane
Stratum spinosum: several layers of polyhedral cells with 'prickle' spines from desmosomes
Stratum granulosum: a few layers of cells packed with basophilic keratohyalin granules
Stratum lucidum: a pale, clear band seen only in thick skin (palms and soles)
Stratum corneum: a thick top layer of flattened, anucleate, keratin-filled squames

images.title: Hand-drawn diagram of keratinised stratified squamous epithelium
images.description: Hand-drawn labelled diagram in a circular field, showing a band of keratin on the surface above squamous, polyhedral and columnar cells. It depicts the keratinised type, so it belongs with the keratinised squamous tissue rather than the non-keratinised one. Its labels read keratin, squamous cells, polyhedral cells and columnar cells, with connective tissue below.
images.author: Veeresh likhitha
images.source_description: Histology of stratified squamous keratinised epithelium consists of keratin layer ,squamous cells,polygonal cells,columnar cells,

tissues.name: Transitional epithelium (urothelium)
tissues.summary: Transitional epithelium, or urothelium, is a stretchable stratified epithelium that lines the urinary tract from the renal calyces to the proximal urethra. Its surface umbrella cells form a barrier that stops urine leaking into the wall, and the layers thin as the organ fills.
features: Large dome-shaped umbrella cells on the luminal surface, some binucleate
About 6–7 cell layers when relaxed, flattening to 2–3 layers when distended
Pear-shaped intermediate cells in the middle layers
Small cuboidal basal cells resting on the lamina propria
Mucosal folds in a contracted specimen that flatten out when the organ is distended

images.title: Urothelium lining mucosal folds, low power
images.description: Low-power view of urothelium lining several mucosal folds, with blue-staining connective tissue beneath and adipose tissue at the bottom of the field. The circular field suggests a camera photo taken through a microscope eyepiece; the stain is not stated, but the blue collagen and red-pink epithelium suggest a trichrome-type stain, and no magnification is given. Students should trace the folded lining and the thin epithelium on each fold, as individual cells are not resolved at this power.
images.author: Beich15
images.source_description: In theory, it is urothelium tissue but I prefer to think that it is a no yet discovered planet.

images.title: Urinary bladder urothelium, H&E stain
images.description: Section through the wall of the urinary bladder showing urothelium with individual cells clearly resolved and the lumen at the top. Large umbrella cells line the surface above several rows of intermediate cells, and smaller basal cells sit on the pink collagen of the lamina propria below. Magnification is not given; students should find the large surface cells with rounded bulges and the fibroblast nuclei in the lamina propria.
images.author: User:Polarlys
images.source_description: urinary bladder, urothelium, haemalum-eosin stain

images.title: Diagram of urothelium layers: umbrella, intermediate and basal cells
images.description: Labelled schematic of bladder urothelium read from the luminal surface down: a GAG mucin layer, one row of large umbrella cells, several rows of intermediate cells and one row of basal cells. It is a drawing rather than a micrograph, so there is no stain or magnification, and the cell shapes are stylised. Students should use it to learn the order of the layers and the relative size of each cell type.

images.source_description: The image shows from top down, the mucin layer of the bladder, the umbrella cells, the intermediate cells, and then the basal cells of the urinary bladdar urothelium.

images.title: Hand-drawn diagram of transitional epithelium: umbrella, pear-shaped and basal cells
images.description: Coloured hand-drawn sketch of a microscope field on a numbered practical page, headed Transitional epithelium. It shows a band of stratified epithelium with three labelled layers: umbrella cells at the surface, pear-shaped cells in the middle and basal cells at the base, above connective tissue drawn with fibres and round profiles. No stain or magnification is given; use it to match the layer order and cell shapes with a slide.
images.author: Roshini5823
images.source_description: Histological diagram of transitional epithelium which is present in urethra , ureter and urinary bladder

images.title: Schematic of transitional epithelium: stacked cell layers on a base line
images.description: Small, low-resolution textbook-style schematic of transitional epithelium, with several rows of nucleated cells: the largest, rounded cells are at the surface and smaller cells lie towards a thin base line at the bottom. images.author: Jmarchn
images.source_description: Transitional epithelium

tissues.name: Stratified cuboidal & columnar epithelium
tissues.summary: Stratified cuboidal and stratified columnar epithelia are uncommon linings made of two or more layers of cells, found mainly in the ducts of larger glands such as sweat glands and large salivary ducts. Their multiple layers make them mainly protective, and they often form transitional zones between other epithelia.
features: Two or more layers of cells, with only the basal layer resting on the basement membrane
Stratified cuboidal type: roughly cube-shaped surface cells in the ducts of sweat glands
Stratified columnar type: tall columnar surface cells above smaller basal cells
Duct lumen lined by several layers of cells, with connective tissue around the duct
Columnar type found in large salivary ducts, conjunctiva and parts of the male urethra
Transitional zones where another epithelium changes into this one

images.title: Stratified cuboidal epithelium lining ducts: stained micrograph
images.description: Stained micrograph of ducts, with a large curved duct in the centre-left and a smaller one at the lower right. The duct walls are several cells thick, with round, purple-stained nuclei and a pale lumen in the middle of each duct. The stain appears to be H&E, and no magnification or organ is given; the source describes the original animation as highlighting nuclei, epithelial cells and underlying connective tissue.
images.author: Laird.sheldahl
images.source_description: Stratified cuboidal epithelium, highlighting the nucleuses, rest of the epithelial cells, and underlying connective tissue

images.title: Stratified cuboidal epithelium: two layers of cells, diagram
images.description: Flat coloured diagram, so there is no stain or magnification. It shows an epithelium two cells deep, with round central nuclei, resting on a purple basement membrane line above pale connective tissue. The cells are broad and polygonal rather than cube-shaped, so students should look for the two stacked layers and the basement membrane rather than the cell shape.
images.author: Jmarchn
images.source_description: Stratified cuboidal epithelium

images.title: Stratified columnar epithelium: two layers of tall cells, diagram
images.description: Flat coloured diagram with no stain or magnification. It shows two stacked layers of tall columnar cells, each with a central oval nucleus, sitting on a purple basement membrane line above pale connective tissue. The basal layer is drawn as tall as the surface layer, which is a simplification because in real stratified columnar epithelium the basal cells are usually smaller; students should look for the two layers and the basement membrane.
images.author: Jmarchn
images.source_description: Stratified colunar epithelium

tissues.name: Pleura & peritoneum (serous membranes)
tissues.summary: Serosa is a serous membrane: a single layer of flat mesothelial cells resting on a thin layer of loose connective tissue, lining body cavities such as the pleura and peritoneum and covering the organs inside them. It secretes a thin serous fluid that lets organs glide smoothly against each other and against the cavity walls.
features: Single layer of flat (simple squamous) mesothelial cells on the free surface
Flattened, oval nuclei that bulge slightly above the cell surface
Thin layer of loose areolar connective tissue directly beneath the mesothelium
Parietal layer lying on skeletal muscle or fat, with blood vessels in the loose tissue
Milky spots (clusters of lymphocytes and macrophages) in the omentum

images.title: Parietal peritoneum over skeletal muscle, Masson trichrome
images.description: Parietal peritoneum appears as a thin pale surface layer over skeletal muscle, with fat cells and blood vessels packed with red blood cells beneath it. tissues.name: Loose (areolar) connective tissue
tissues.summary: Loose (areolar) connective tissue is a cell-rich connective tissue with thin, loosely arranged collagen and elastic fibres in abundant hydrated ground substance. It forms the lamina propria under epithelia and surrounds vessels and nerves, and it is the site of oedema and of the early inflammatory response.
features: Fibroblasts, the most common cells, with oval or spindle-shaped nuclei
Thin collagen fibres forming a loose mesh rather than dense bundles
Fine, wavy elastic fibres, thinner than the collagen fibres
Pale ground substance filling the spaces between the fibres
Macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells and leukocytes scattered among the fibroblasts
Lamina propria under epithelia and around vessels and nerves

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: very blurred field

tissues.name: Dense regular connective tissue
tissues.summary: Dense regular connective tissue is made of parallel bundles of type I collagen, which give great tensile strength in one direction. It forms tendons, ligaments and aponeuroses, with fibroblasts (tenocytes in tendon) lying in rows between the bundles.
features: Parallel collagen bundles that all run in one direction
Wavy (crimped) collagen that straightens under load
Rows of flattened fibroblast (tenocyte) nuclei squeezed between the bundles
Few cells overall, so the tissue looks almost uniformly pink in H&E
Looser connective tissue (epitenon) at the margins

tissues.name: Dense irregular connective tissue
tissues.summary: Dense irregular connective tissue is made mainly of thick collagen fibre bundles that run in many directions, so it resists stress applied from any side. It forms the reticular dermis of the skin and the capsules of organs, periosteum, perichondrium and dura mater, and it has relatively few cells.
features: Thick collagen bundles interlacing in many directions, not in parallel layers
Few cells: small, spindle-shaped fibroblast nuclei scattered between the bundles
Elastic fibres, where stained, forming a fine dark network among the collagen
Found in the reticular dermis of skin and in organ capsules, periosteum, perichondrium and dura mater
Contrast with dense regular tissue, where the bundles run parallel in one direction

images.title: Dense irregular connective tissue: collagen bundles in many directions, H&E

tissues.name: Adipose tissue
tissues.summary: Adipose tissue is loose connective tissue specialised for storing energy as fat in adipocytes, and it also secretes hormones such as leptin and adiponectin. White fat holds one large lipid droplet per cell, while brown fat has many small droplets and heat-producing mitochondria.
features: Unilocular white adipocytes: one large lipid droplet pushes the nucleus to the rim (signet-ring appearance)
Lipid is dissolved during processing, so the cells look pale and empty
Thin connective tissue septa with small nuclei divide the fat into lobules
Brown fat: many small lipid droplets and many mitochondria, mainly in neonates
Rich capillary network running between the adipocytes

tissues.name: Reticular connective tissue
tissues.summary: Reticular connective tissue is a fine, branching meshwork of type III collagen fibres made by reticular cells (specialised fibroblasts). It forms the supporting framework of lymphoid and haematopoietic organs such as lymph nodes, spleen and bone marrow.
features: Fine, branching reticular fibres forming a delicate three-dimensional mesh
Fibres are argyrophilic: they turn black with silver stains and are faint in H&E
Reticular cells (fibroblast-like, with long processes) lying along the fibres
Mesh filled with lymphocytes or blood-forming cells in lymph node, spleen and bone marrow
Fibres wrap around blood vessels and sinuses within the organ

tissues.name: Hyaline cartilage
tissues.summary: Hyaline cartilage is the most common type of cartilage, a glassy, avascular tissue whose matrix is rich in type II collagen and aggrecan. It covers articular surfaces, forms the costal cartilages and airway rings, and acts as the template for long-bone growth at the growth plate.
features: Glassy, homogeneous matrix with no visible collagen fibres in routine H&E sections
Chondrocytes sit in lacunae, often in isogenous groups
Basophilic territorial matrix around each cell group, rich in aggrecan
Perichondrium: dense fibrous sheath with flattened cells, present except on articular surfaces
Avascular: no blood vessels in the matrix, so nutrients diffuse through it

tissues.name: Elastic cartilage
tissues.summary: Elastic cartilage is a flexible cartilage whose matrix holds a dense network of elastic fibres alongside collagen, so it can bend and then spring back to shape. It forms the auricle of the ear, the epiglottis, the external acoustic meatus and the auditory tube.
features: Dense network of elastic fibres in the matrix, staining dark with orcein or Verhoeff stains
Chondrocytes sitting in lacunae within the matrix
A perichondrium (dense fibrous layer) around the cartilage, as in hyaline cartilage
Found in the auricle of the ear, epiglottis, external acoustic meatus and auditory tube

tissues.name: Fibrocartilage
tissues.summary: Fibrocartilage is a tough, transitional form of cartilage in which thick bundles of type I collagen run between rows of fibrochondrocytes. It resists both compression and tension, and is found in the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci and labra.
features: Thick, dense bundles of type I collagen, often wavy and running in parallel
Fibrochondrocytes in rows between the collagen bundles, sitting in small lacunae
No perichondrium: the tissue merges straight into the surrounding dense connective tissue
Gradual transition where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone (enthesis)
Found in the annulus fibrosus of intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci and labra

images.description: Cross section of fibrocartilage at 40x magnification, stained blue; the stain is not named in the source, but the strong blue collagen suggests a trichrome. tissues.name: Compact (cortical) bone
tissues.summary: Compact (cortical) bone is the dense outer layer of bone, built from osteons whose concentric lamellae wrap around a central canal carrying blood vessels and nerves. It gives bone its strength and stiffness, with osteocytes sitting in lacunae linked by canaliculi.
features: Concentric lamellae wrapped around a central (Haversian) canal holding vessels and nerves
Osteocytes sitting in lacunae, linked by canaliculi
Perforating (Volkmann) canals running across the osteons to join central canals
Circumferential and interstitial lamellae filling the gaps between osteons
Outer surface covered by periosteum, with Sharpey fibres entering the bone

images.title: Compact bone: osteon in a polarised ground section
images.description: Human bone cross-section that appears to be an unstained ground section, with colour fringes suggesting polarised light; a 0.1 mm scale bar is shown. One osteon sits in the centre, with its dark central canal ringed by concentric lamellae. Look for the central canal, the dark lacunae scattered through the lamellae and the fine canaliculi between them.

A single osteon lies in the centre, with a dark central canal and concentric lamellae around it, and dark lacunae scattered across the surrounding bone. Use it to see the lamellar rings of an osteon and the lacunae that house the osteocytes.

tissues.name: Spongy (cancellous) bone
tissues.summary: Spongy (cancellous) bone is a porous lattice of trabeculae, thin bony plates and rods, with marrow filling the spaces between them; it forms the interior of the epiphyses, vertebral bodies and flat bones. Its trabeculae are aligned along the lines of mechanical stress, giving strength for low weight and a large surface for bone remodelling.
features: Trabeculae of lamellar bone with no osteons, so no central canals
Osteocytes in lacunae within the trabeculae, linked by canaliculi
Cuboidal osteoblasts lining surfaces where new bone is being laid down
Multinucleated osteoclasts in Howship lacunae on resorbing surfaces
Marrow spaces between trabeculae, holding fat and haematopoietic cells

images.title: Spongy bone: trabecular lattice with marrow spaces (illustration)
images.description: Stylised vector illustration of normal spongy bone, drawn as a lattice of cream bony trabeculae enclosing rounded tan and dark marrow spaces. It is a schematic rather than a stained section, so no stain or magnification applies. Students should see that the trabeculae form one continuous three-dimensional network, with marrow filling the gaps between them.

The source does not name the stain, but in panel A the bone is magenta-purple, with marrow cells as dark dots and fat cells as clear white spaces. In panel B the trabeculae show bright blue and pink birefringence, which reflects the ordered collagen of lamellar bone.

tissues.name: Bone development & growth plate
tissues.summary: Bone forms in two ways: intramembranous ossification lays down bone directly within mesenchyme, while endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model. The epiphyseal growth plate is the cartilage zone that drives longitudinal growth of long bones.
features: Growth plate zones in order: resting, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcified, then bone
Proliferative zone: flattened chondrocytes stacked in neat columns
Hypertrophic zone: enlarged chondrocytes in lacunae, with thin calcified septa between columns
Intramembranous bone: trabeculae forming directly in vascular mesenchyme, with no cartilage model
Osteoblasts lining new bone, osteocytes in lacunae, osteoclasts in resorption pits

images.title: Chondrogenous ossification: bone forming from a cartilage model
images.description: Section of chondrogenous ossification, where bone replaces a cartilage model, stained with trichrome (the source describes blue staining). Pale chondrocytes in lacunae sit on the right, with a blue band of matrix between them and red-stained cells on the left. Students should compare the cartilage cells with the newly laid bone matrix beside them.

images.title: Desmogenous ossification: bone forming directly in fibrous tissue

Students should look for this bone surrounded by loose, pale connective tissue.

images.title: Intramembranous ossification: labelled diagram in four panels
images.description: Labelled teaching diagram from Anatomy and Physiology (Connexions), with panels a to d. tissues.name: Bone marrow
tissues.summary: Bone marrow is the soft tissue filling bone cavities, where haematopoietic stem cells produce red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells. Red marrow carries out this blood formation, while yellow marrow is mainly fat.
features: Cords of developing blood cells lying between wide, thin-walled sinusoids
Megakaryocytes: the largest marrow cells, with lobed nuclei, releasing platelets into the sinusoids
Erythroblastic islands: erythroid precursors with round nuclei clustered around a central macrophage
Granulocyte precursors with granular cytoplasm, such as eosinophil myelocytes with orange-red granules
Clear fat cells (adipocytes), which increase with age as red marrow turns yellow

images.author: Magnon, C. and Frenette, P.S., Hematopoietic stem cell trafficking (July 14, 2008), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.8.1, http://www.stembook.org.
images.source_title: HSC migration from embryonic to fetal hematopoiesis.
images.source_description: Definitive hematopoietic stem cell pools emerge from intra- (AGM) and extra- (yolk sac and placenta) embryonic hematopoietic sites. When the circulation is established and functional, HSCs start their migratory journey and colonize the placenta, followed by the fetal liver that becomes the major hematopoietic organ until the bone marrow colonized by HSCs. The adhesion molecule VE-cadherin expression has been suggested to participate in HSC/progenitor migration but there is no functional data about the molecular mediators of HSC migration in the embryo. The colonization of the fetal liver and the bone marrow are dependent on β1 integrins and the CXCL12/CXCR4 chemokine/receptor axis.

tissues.name: Blood cells
tissues.summary: Blood is a fluid connective tissue in which erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets are suspended in plasma. In a stained smear the erythrocytes are by far the most numerous cells, with white cells and platelets scattered among them.
features: Erythrocytes: anucleate biconcave discs, about 7.5 µm, the most numerous cells and a size reference
Neutrophils (40–70% of white cells): multilobed nucleus with fine granules
Lymphocytes (20–40%): round, dense nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm
Monocytes: large cell with a kidney-shaped nucleus; they become macrophages in tissue
Eosinophils: bilobed nucleus with red granules; basophils: dark purple granules
Platelets: small anucleate fragments, 2–3 µm across

tissues.name: Skeletal muscle
tissues.summary: Skeletal muscle is made of long, multinucleated, cross-striated fibres under voluntary control, which contract to move the skeleton. Each fibre forms by fusion of precursor cells, so its nuclei sit at the edge, just beneath the sarcolemma.
features: Oval nuclei pushed to the edge of each fibre; central nuclei suggest pathology or regeneration
Cross-striations: dark A bands, light I bands and Z lines form the sarcomeres, seen at high power
Connective tissue sheaths: endomysium around each fibre, perimysium around fascicles, epimysium around the whole muscle
Satellite cells lie beneath the basal lamina and allow limited regeneration
Type I (slow, oxidative) and type II (fast, glycolytic) fibres intermix within the muscle

tissues.name: Cardiac muscle (myocardium)
tissues.summary: Cardiac muscle forms the thick muscular wall of the heart (the myocardium) and contracts rhythmically without conscious control. Its branched, striated fibres are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which let them contract as one coordinated unit.
features: Branched, cross-striated fibres that link end to end in chains
One or two central nuclei per fibre, with a pale zone around each nucleus
Intercalated discs: dark, step-like transverse lines where neighbouring fibres meet
Abundant mitochondria (about a third of cell volume) and a rich capillary network between fibres
Purkinje fibres: large pale conducting cells lying beneath the endocardium

tissues.name: Smooth muscle
tissues.summary: Smooth muscle is non-striated muscle made of spindle-shaped cells, each with one central nucleus, that forms the walls of hollow organs, blood vessels and airways, and is also found in the iris. Its involuntary contraction moves contents along the gut and changes the diameter of vessels and airways.
features: Spindle-shaped cells, each with one central, cigar-shaped nucleus
No cross-striations, unlike skeletal and cardiac muscle
Nuclei that corkscrew when the cells contract
Parallel sheets of fibres in the walls of gut, vessels, airways and uterus

tissues.name: Peripheral nerve
tissues.summary: Peripheral nerves are bundles of myelinated and unmyelinated axons, grouped into fascicles and wrapped in three connective-tissue sheaths: epineurium, perineurium and endoneurium. They carry nerve impulses between the central nervous system and the rest of the body.
features: Epineurium: dense connective tissue around the whole nerve, containing fat and blood vessels
Perineurium: flattened cell layers around each fascicle, forming the blood-nerve barrier
Endoneurium: delicate connective tissue between the individual axons inside each fascicle
Myelinated axons: round profiles with pale halos in H&E sections
Blood vessels: lie in the epineurium and beside the fascicles

tissues.name: Sensory & autonomic ganglia
tissues.summary: Ganglia are clusters of nerve cell bodies lying outside the central nervous system. Sensory (dorsal root) ganglia carry signals from the body into the spinal cord, while autonomic ganglia relay signals from the CNS to glands, smooth muscle and the heart.
features: Dorsal root ganglion: large round sensory neurons packed together, each ringed by small satellite cells
Autonomic ganglia: smaller multipolar neurons with eccentric nuclei, set among nerve fibres
A large round nucleus with a prominent nucleolus in each neuron
Nissl substance (granular basophilic cytoplasm) in the neuron cell bodies, clearest with cresyl violet
Bundles of wavy nerve fibres (axons) running into or out of the ganglion, with a connective tissue capsule

images.title: Earthworm nerve ganglion stained green, with recording pins through it

Two metal recording pins pass through the tissue, the source says it was mishandled during imaging, and no magnification is given, so the cell detail is poor.
images.author: Erin Asadourian
images.source_description: This ganglion came from Lumbricus terrestris, or a leech. It was used during the BIPN 145 neurobiology lab at the University of California, San Diego. Intracellular recording were captured from individual neurons in the ganglion using glass pipette and action potentials were recorded. The neuron was also stimulated to induce action potentials as well. The final thing done to the ganglion was to stain it with Alexa Fluor 488 green dye, this is why the ganglion appears green. Unfortunately the ganglion was mishandled during the imaging which is why you can see the anchors, the two metal rods stuck through the ganglion.

tissues.name: Elastic artery (aorta)
tissues.summary: The elastic artery is a large conducting vessel, such as the aorta and its major branches, whose tunica media is built from many concentric elastic lamellae with smooth muscle between them. Its elastic recoil stores energy during systole and keeps blood moving through diastole.
features: Tunica media of 40-70 wavy, fenestrated elastic lamellae stacked concentrically
Smooth muscle nuclei lying between the elastic lamellae in the media
Verhoeff stain: elastic lamellae dark purple to black against pale interlamellar spaces
Media forms most of the wall thickness, unlike the smooth-muscle-dominated muscular artery
Vasa vasorum: small vessels that supply the outer part of the thick wall

images.title: Aortic wall in H&E at low power, seen through a microscope eyepiece
images.description: Photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece, showing a low-power view of the aortic wall in H&E. A dense pink band of media curves across the upper half of the circular field, with paler, looser tissue at the lower left. Students should note the parallel, layered arrangement of the wall rather than any single cell.

images.title: Elastic lamellae in the aortic wall, Verhoeff stain
images.description: Aortic wall stained with Verhoeff's elastic stain, which colours elastic fibres dark purple to black on a pale background. tissues.name: Muscular arteries & arterioles
tissues.summary: Muscular (distributing) arteries carry blood to organs and have a thick media of smooth muscle bounded by distinct internal and external elastic laminae. Their smaller branches, the arterioles, are the main site of peripheral resistance and so help set blood pressure.
features: Wavy internal elastic lamina separating the intima from the media
Thick media of many circular layers of smooth muscle, the bulk of the wall
External elastic lamina at the outer edge of the media
Collagen-rich adventitia outside the external elastic lamina
Arterioles with only 1-2 layers of smooth muscle in the media

images.title: Muscular artery in cross section, trichrome-type stain
images.description: Bright-field photomicrograph of a whole cross section of a human artery, with fat and small neighbouring profiles around it. The source does not name the stain, but the blue collagen in the outer coat and the purple-red media suggest a trichrome stain, and no magnification is given. images.author: en:User:Stijn Ghesquiere, user:Drsrisenthil, Furfur (German translation and slight adaption)
images.source_title: Microscopic anatomy of an artery de
images.source_description: Microscopic anatomy of an artery. The outermost layer is known as tunica adventitia, and is composed of connective tissue made up of collagen fibers. Inside this layer is the tunica media, or media, which is made up of smooth muscle cells and elastic tissue (also called connective tissue proper). The innermost layer, which is in direct contact with the flow of blood, is the tunica intima, commonly called the intima. This layer is mainly made up of endothelial cells. The hollow internal cavity in which the blood flows is called the lumen.

images.title: Diagram of artery wall layers with English labels

images.author: Stijn Ghesquiere, Drsrisenthil
images.source_title: Microscopic anatomy of an artery en
images.source_description:
Microscopic anatomy of an artery. The outermost layer is known as tunica adventitia, and is composed of connective tissue made up of collagen fibers. Inside this layer is the tunica media, or media, which is made up of smooth muscle cells and elastic tissue (also called connective tissue proper).
The innermost layer, which is in direct contact with the flow of blood, is the tunica intima, commonly called the intima. This layer is mainly made up of endothelial cells. The hollow internal cavity in which the blood flows is called the lumen.

tissues.name: Veins & venules
tissues.summary: Veins and venules carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, and because they hold much of the body's blood they act as capacitance vessels. Their walls are thin, with a thin media and a thick adventitia, and the larger veins, especially in the limbs, have valves that stop blood flowing backwards.
features: Large, thin-walled lumen, often collapsed in sections, compared with the accompanying artery
Thin media with far less smooth muscle than the accompanying artery
Adventitia (outer coat) is the thickest layer of the wall
Valves: pocket-shaped folds of intima in limb veins that stop backflow
Venules: very thin wall, and the site where leukocytes leave the blood in inflammation

tissues.name: Capillaries & sinusoids
tissues.summary: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, a single thin layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane, where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissue. Their walls are continuous, fenestrated or sinusoidal (discontinuous) depending on the organ, and pericytes wrap their outer surface to help regulate flow.
features: Thin wall of flat endothelial cells, with nuclei bulging into a narrow lumen
Lumen often just wide enough for one red blood cell
Pericytes: small cells outside the endothelium, within the basement membrane
Fenestrations: pores through the endothelium, seen only on electron microscopy
Sinusoids: wide, irregular channels with gaps between endothelial cells (liver, spleen)
Continuous type: tight junctions seal the endothelium (muscle, CNS)

images.title: Capillary bed with its arterioles and venules (schematic, Spanish labels)
images.description: Labelled schematic illustration (not a microscope image) of a capillary bed, showing an arteriole feeding a network of capillaries through a metarteriole and precapillary sphincters, which drains into a venule. A thoroughfare channel and an arteriovenous anastomosis provide direct routes from arteriole to venule that bypass the capillaries. Students should trace blood flow from the arteriole through the capillaries to the venule, and note where the precapillary sphincters control entry into the capillaries.

images.source_description: Esquema en el que pueden observarse los capilares sanguíneos, metarteriolas, arteriolas, vénulas y esfinter precapilar.

images.title: Fenestrated capillary wall: cutaway schematic (Spanish labels)
images.description: Labelled cutaway schematic (not a microscope image) of a fenestrated capillary, showing the basement membrane on the outside, the endothelium on the inside, and tight junctions between endothelial cells. Round fenestrations (pores) pierce the endothelium across the wall. Students should find these pores, which let fluid and small molecules pass quickly in organs such as the kidney glomerulus and endocrine glands.

images.title: Capillary with a red blood cell in pancreatic tissue, electron micrograph

Students should find the thin endothelial lining, which the source describes as fenestrated, and the dark, crescent-shaped red blood cell.

images.source_title: A red blood cell in a capillary, pancreatic tissue - TEM

Note the abundance of rough endoplasmic reticulum in the acinar cells. There is a red blood cell within the capillary. The capillary lining consists of long, thin endothelial cells, connected by tight junctions. The image shows fenestration of these endothelial cells. The image also shows synaptic vesicles in the neuron(nerve cell) next to the capillary.

images.title: Neurovascular unit: capillary wall with pericytes, astrocytes and neurons
images.description: Labelled diagram (not a microscope image) of the neurovascular unit in the brain, showing a cross section of a capillary with a single endothelial layer joined by tight junctions, pericytes and basement membrane, surrounded by astrocyte endfeet. Neurons, an interneuron, an astrocyte and microglia sit nearby, and astrocytes signal to the capillary to change blood flow. Students should name the layers of the capillary wall and see how the endothelial tight junctions form the blood-brain barrier.
images.author: Brown LS, Foster CG, Courtney J-M, King NE, Howells DW and Sutherland BA
images.source_title: The cellular components of the neurovascular unit
images.source_description: Figure 2. The cellular components of the neurovascular unit (NVU). The capillary wall contains a single EC layer (green) connected by tight junctions that form the blood-brain barrier along with pericytes (red), that are embedded within the capillary basement membrane (light blue), and nearby astrocyte endfeet (yellow). Excitatory neurons (blue) synapse with both vasoactive interneurons (purple), and astrocytes (yellow), who in turn signal to the capillary to alter blood flow according to the metabolic demands of that brain region. Microglia (indigo) are located in the brain parenchyma and respond to any aversive stimuli to protect the brain.

images.title: Control and diabetic retinal capillaries, showing pericyte loss
images.description: Medical illustration (not a microscope image) comparing a healthy eye with one affected by diabetic retinopathy, with close-ups of retinal capillaries. In the control, the capillary is wrapped by pericytes and carries red blood cells, while in diabetes pericytes are lost or degenerate, leading to microaneurysms, fluid spill and bleeding. Students should identify the pericytes on the capillary and see how losing them weakens the vessel wall.
images.author: Laredo F, Plebanski J and Tedeschi A
images.source_description: Figure 3. Diabetic retinopathy. During the early stages of diabetic retinopathy, pericytes loss weakens blood capillaries in the retina, causing the formation of microaneurysms, fluid spill and bleeding into the macula. As diabetic retinopathy progresses, the growth of new and irregular blood vessels leads to the formation of a scar tissue that causes blurry vision and loss of eyesight. Created with biorender.com.

tissues.name: Heart valves, endocardium & pericardium
tissues.summary: The heart valves are thin, essentially avascular flaps of dense connective tissue covered by endothelium, opening and closing to keep blood flowing one way through the heart. The endocardium lines the heart chambers and valves, while the epicardium (visceral pericardium) is the outer mesothelial layer over fat and coronary vessels.
features: Valve cusp: fibrosa, spongiosa and ventricularis/atrialis layers of dense connective tissue, essentially avascular
Endocardium: thin endothelial lining over subendothelial connective tissue
Subendocardium: loose connective tissue containing Purkinje fibres, which are large, pale-staining cells
Epicardium (visceral pericardium): mesothelium over fat containing coronary vessels
Rheumatic fever: scarred, fused valve commissures and Aschoff bodies

Students should find the thin endothelial lining, the loose connective tissue beneath it and the large, pale-staining Purkinje fibre in the subendocardium.

tissues.name: Lymph node
tissues.summary: The lymph node is an encapsulated organ on the lymphatic route that filters lymph and starts immune responses to the antigens it carries. Its outer cortex holds B-cell follicles, the paracortex holds T cells and high endothelial venules, and the medulla holds cords of plasma cells and medullary sinuses.
features: Thin fibrous capsule with a pale subcapsular sinus just beneath it
Cortex: B-cell follicles, some with pale germinal centres
Paracortex: diffuse T-cell zone with high endothelial venules
Medulla: medullary cords of plasma cells and medullary sinuses
Trabeculae: fibrous septa carrying vessels in from the capsule
Reticular fibres and fibroblastic reticular cells forming a meshwork

tissues.name: Spleen
tissues.summary: The spleen is a lymphoid organ that filters the blood. Its white pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens, while its red pulp removes old and damaged red blood cells.
features: White pulp: lymphoid nodules around central arterioles, with pale germinal centres in B-cell follicles
Marginal zone: a ring of cells at the edge of the white pulp, where it meets the red pulp
Red pulp: splenic cords between wide, blood-filled sinusoids
Sinusoids lined by elongated, stave-like endothelial cells
Fibrous capsule with trabeculae carrying vessels into the organ
Brown haemosiderin pigment in red pulp macrophages

tissues.name: Thymus
tissues.summary: The thymus is the primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature, organised into lobules. Each lobule has a dense outer cortex packed with developing thymocytes and a paler medulla containing Hassall's corpuscles.
features: Lobules divided by connective tissue septa, each with a dark cortex and paler medulla
Cortex densely packed with small thymocytes (developing T cells)
Medulla paler, with fewer lymphocytes and more epithelial cells
Hassall's (thymic) corpuscles: concentric whorls of epithelial cells in the medulla
No lymphoid follicles or germinal centres in the normal thymus
Adult thymus involutes, with lymphoid tissue progressively replaced by fat

tissues.name: Tonsils (Waldeyer's ring)
tissues.summary: The tonsils are partially encapsulated lymphoid tissues lying beneath the pharyngeal epithelium as part of Waldeyer's ring. The palatine tonsil is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium that dips into crypts, while the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) is covered by respiratory epithelium.
features: Palatine tonsil: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium dipping into deep crypts
Numerous lymphoid follicles with pale germinal centres and dark mantle zones
Tingible body macrophages with apoptotic debris inside germinal centres
Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid): covered by pseudostratified ciliated respiratory epithelium

images.title: Adenoid: several lymphoid follicles beneath the surface epithelium
images.description: Low-power H&E view of adenoid tissue showing several lymphoid follicles, each with a paler germinal centre and a darker rim of small lymphocytes. images.title: Adenoid germinal centre: tingible body macrophages with apoptotic debris

tissues.name: Thin (hairy) skin
tissues.summary: Thin (hairy) skin covers most of the body: a keratinised stratified squamous epidermis with no stratum lucidum sits over a dermis of papillary and reticular connective tissue that contains hair follicles and glands, with a hypodermis of adipose tissue beneath. It protects the body and, through its sensory receptors, hair, sweat glands and blood supply, helps detect touch and temperature and regulate body heat.
features: Keratinised stratified squamous epidermis with no stratum lucidum
Hair follicles with hair shafts, sebaceous glands and arrector pili muscles in the dermis
Papillary dermis of loose connective tissue above reticular dermis of dense irregular connective tissue
Melanocytes in the basal layer, which pass melanin to the keratinocytes
Sweat glands and blood vessels in the dermis
Hypodermis of adipose tissue beneath the dermis

images.title: Historical image of a single dendritic (Langerhans) cell with branching processes
images.description: Black and white image of a single cell with long branching processes, captioned as a dendritic cell by Paul Langerhans. The source gives no stain or magnification. It shows a Langerhans cell, an epidermal dendritic cell, rather than an islet cell, so it belongs with the skin.

images.title: Schematic of a Langerhans cell in the epidermis, macrophage and dendritic features
images.description: Diagram, not a micrograph, of the epidermis from the stratum basale to the stratum corneum, with a Langerhans cell in the stratum spinosum. Green labels mark macrophage features such as self-renewal and embryonic origin, and red labels mark dendritic cell features such as antigen presentation and migration to lymph nodes. No stain, as it is a diagram.
images.author: Deckers J, Hammad H and Hoste E
images.source_title: Schematic representation of the properties of Langerhans cell (LC) shared by dendritic cells (DCs) or macrophages
images.source_description: Figure 1. Schematic representation of the properties of Langerhans cell (LC) shared by dendritic cells (DCs) or macrophages. LCs display a mixture of properties, which they share with macrophages (indicated in green), such as self-maintenance and ontogeny. However, LCs are capable of presenting antigen and actively migrate to the draining lymph nodes, which qualifies them as DCs (properties shared between LCs and DCs are indicated in red).

images.title: Langerhans cell roles in the skin and after migration to the lymph node
images.description: Figure 1 diagram, not a micrograph, comparing Langerhans cell functions in the skin (left, within the epidermis) with migratory functions in a lymph node (right). Green boxes mark known functions and red boxes mark potential functions, and the T cell types involved are shown in the key. It is a diagram of skin immunology, not of islets, so it belongs with the skin.
images.author: West HC and Bennett CL
images.source_title: Diagram illustrating known and predicted skin resident versus migratory roles for Langerhans cells (LC).
images.source_description: Figure 1. Diagram illustrating known and predicted skin resident versus migratory roles for Langerhans cells (LC). LC have important functions as resident cells in the skin and as migratory cells to the lymph nodes (LN). Studies have largely focused on their potential importance in priming T cell immunity in LN; however, it is now appreciated that LC have many functions in situ in the skin. Demonstrated functions (shown in green) in the skin include interaction with resident memory T cells, clearance of apoptotic keratinocytes, licensing of effector T cell function, sentinel functions, and interaction with regulatory T cells. Data further suggest the potential for other macrophage-like functions of LC such as a role in the polarization of CD4+ T cells in situ (shown in red).

images.title: Langerhans cells in epidermal sheets and their dendrite counts
images.description: Figure 3 with a micrograph of two Langerhans cells in epidermal sheets (panel A, scale bar 10 micrometres), where brown cell processes stand out against a blue-purple background, and bar charts of dendrites per cell (panels B to D). The stain is not named in the source. Students should count the dendrites on cells i and ii, and see how counts differ between untreated and treated skin and between pre-culture and post-culture at 24 and 48 hours.
images.author: M, Kang S-M, Song J-M, Anstey AV, Ivory M, Compans RW, et al.
images.source_title: Number of dendrites per LC in epidermal sheets
images.source_description:
Figure 3. Number of dendrites per LC in epidermal sheets.

(A) Microscopic examination revealed each LC to have a distinct cell body from which dendrites protruded (bar = 10µm). Two individual LCs designated (i) and (ii) with 4 and 5 dendrites per cell, indicated by the white and red arrows, respectively. Percentage frequency of dendrites per LC in (B) pre-cultured epidermal sheets and post-cultured epidermal sheets at 24 (C) and 48 (D) hours; untreated skin (black bars), skin treated with H1 VLPs delivered by ID injection (white bars). Data presented as mean ± SEM (n = 8).

tissues.name: Thick (glabrous) skin
tissues.summary: Thick, hairless skin of the palms and soles, with a very thick keratinised epidermis that has five layers, including a stratum lucidum. Its thick epidermis and deep epidermal ridges resist friction and abrasion on these weight-bearing surfaces.
features: Very thick stratum corneum with a distinct, pale stratum lucidum beneath it
Deep epidermal ridges (rete pegs) projecting between dermal papillae
No hair follicles or sebaceous glands in the section
Eccrine sweat ducts coiling through the epidermis
Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae, close under the basal layer
structures: Palmar surfaces of digits of hand
Plantar surfaces of digits of foot

images.title: Thick skin: epidermis and dermis at low power
images.description: Low-power view of a thick skin section stained with H&E, as stated in the source; no magnification is given. The pink epidermis is thick and forms downward ridges between upward dermal papillae, sitting on the pale, wavy collagen of the dermis. A crack or fold artefact runs through the epidermis in the centre of the field.

images.source_description: microscopic view of the thick skin stained with H&E

images.title: Thick skin: thick keratin layer over epidermis and dermal papillae
images.description: Higher-power section of thick skin that appears to be H&E-stained; the source gives no stain or magnification. The thick, pale keratinised layer at the top is the stratum corneum, and beneath it the nucleated pink keratinocytes of the epidermis sit above a darker basal layer. Dark basal cells line dermal papillae that project up into the loose dermis, and no hypodermis is visible.

images.source_title: Thick Skin Histological Section (epidermis, dermis and hypodermis)

images.title: Thick skin: thick epidermis with ridges over dermis, low power

images.title: Thick skin (a) compared with thin skin (b), H&E sections
images.description: Two micrographs labelled (a) and (b), each with a small low-power inset, appearing to be H&E-stained; no magnification is given. Panel (a) is thick skin, with a broad, dark epidermis under a keratinised surface layer and deep, thick epidermal ridges reaching into the dermis. Panel (b) is thin skin, with a flat epidermis only a few cells thick over dense pink dermis, so students can compare the depth of the ridges and the thickness of the epidermis.

images.title: Thick skin epidermis: labelled diagram of its five layers
images.description: Labelled teaching diagram of a section through thick skin, from the dermis up to the stratum corneum. It shows the five epidermal layers in order (stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum and corneum), with keratin-filled dead cells at the surface, and the melanocyte, Merkel cell and sensory neuron in the basal region. Students should learn the order of the layers and that the stratum lucidum is found in thick skin.

images.source_description: The epidermis of thick skin has five layers: stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum, and stratum corneum.

tissues.name: Hair follicle & sebaceous gland
tissues.summary: The hair follicle is a down-growth of epidermis into the dermis that makes the hair shaft from matrix cells at its bulb, which caps the dermal papilla. Attached sebaceous glands release sebum into the follicle, and arrector pili smooth muscle erects the hair.
features: Hair bulb: matrix cells capping the dermal papilla at the base of the follicle
Hair shaft: keratinised central core, often pale in sections
Inner and outer root sheaths: nucleated epithelium wrapping the hair shaft
Sebaceous glands: clusters of pale, foamy cells opening into the follicle
Arrector pili: thin smooth muscle band running from the follicle to the dermis
Bulge: swelling of the outer root sheath where follicular stem cells sit

images.author: Gaelle, L. and Cédric, B., Medical applications of epidermal stem cells (November 15, 2008), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.27.1, http://www.stembook.
images.source_title: Hair follicle and inter-follicular epidermis morphogenesis.
images.source_description: The hair follicle growth is stimulated by the dermal papilla (DP) signals, activating the bulge stem cells (Bu) to form the distinct lineages of the hair follicle (HF). Several concentric layers composed the HF. The external and basal layer, called outer root sheath (ORS) maintains contact with the basal layer of the inter-follicular epidermis (IFE). At the base of the HF, the matrix cells (Mx) represent the highly proliferative cells, which differentiate in concentric rings that give rise to the Hair shaft (HS) and its channel the inner root sheath (IRS) and the companion layer. The HF contains also the sebaceous gland (SG), which produces the waterproof sebum. In the left panel, skin was co-stained for the basal cells using the anti-keratin14 antibody (red) and for the bulge SC using the anti–CD34 antibody (green). In the right panel, skin was co-stained for the basal cells using the anti-β4 antibody (white), for the Mx cells using the anti–KI67 antibody (red) and for the HS precursors using the anti-AE13 antibody (green). Nuclei were marked using DAPI staining. Abbreviations used: Bu: bulge stem cells, Der: dermis, DP: dermal papilla, IFE: inter-follicular epidermis, IRS: inner root sheath, HF: hair follicle, HG: hair germ, HS: hair shaft, IRS: inner root sheath, Mx: matrix cells, ORS: outer root sheath, SG: sebaceous gland.

tissues.name: Sweat glands
tissues.summary: Sweat glands are exocrine glands in the dermis that release sweat through ducts onto the skin surface. Eccrine glands, found over most of the body, produce watery sweat for thermoregulation, while apocrine glands in the axilla and groin open into hair follicles.
features: Eccrine secretory coil: a coiled tube of clear and dark cells, with myoepithelial cells around it, lying deep in the dermis
Eccrine duct: two layers of cuboidal cells that stain darker than the secretory coil, running up to the epidermis
Apocrine gland: wide lumens with secretion pinched off from the apical part of the cell
Apocrine glands open into the upper part of hair follicles rather than onto the skin surface
Myoepithelial cells: flattened contractile cells lying outside the secretory cells of both gland types

It is a diagram, so no stain or magnification applies; students should find the secretory granules, the crown-shaped Golgi region and the pinched-off apical portion.

tissues.name: Skin sensory receptors
tissues.summary: Sensory receptors of the skin that respond to touch, pressure, vibration and stretch. Most are encapsulated mechanoreceptor endings in the dermis and hypodermis, such as the Meissner, Pacinian and Ruffini corpuscles.
features: Meissner corpuscle: small oval of stacked flattened cells filling a dermal papilla just beneath the epidermis
Pacinian corpuscle: large onion-like rings of concentric lamellae around a central core, in the deep dermis or hypodermis
Ruffini ending: spindle-shaped capsule in the dermis with branching nerve endings inside
Dermal papillae: finger-like dermal projections pushing up into the epidermis, where the Meissner corpuscles sit
Adipose tissue: Pacinian corpuscles lie among fat cells and small blood vessels in the hypodermis

tissues.name: Nail
tissues.summary: The nail is a plate of hard keratin on the dorsal tip of each finger and toe, protecting the distal digit and supporting fine touch and grip. It is produced by the nail matrix under the proximal nail fold, and the plate slides forward over the nail bed.
features: Nail plate: compact layers of hard keratin with no visible nuclei
Nail matrix: proliferating epidermis under the proximal nail fold that produces the plate
Nail bed: thin epidermis lacking a granular layer, sitting on a dermis with longitudinal ridges
Eponychium: thin keratinised layer of the proximal nail fold that seals the nail root
Lunula: pale crescent at the base of the plate, the visible distal matrix

images.title: Nail and nail groove: longitudinal section diagram
images.description: Labelled line drawing of a longitudinal section through the nail and its nail groove (sulcus), with the eponychium at the proximal fold. It is a drawing rather than a microscope image, so there is no stain or magnification. Students should trace the nail plate within its groove, the epidermal layers (stratum corneum, stratum granulosum, stratum mucosum), and the blood vessels in the corium.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Longitudinal section through nail and its nail groove (sulcus).

tissues.name: Lip & oral mucosa
tissues.summary: Lip and oral mucosa is the moist, stratified squamous lining of the mouth, resting on a lamina propria of connective tissue. It protects the underlying tissue from friction and microbes, changing from keratinised skin on the outer lip to non-keratinised lining inside the mouth.
features: Skin side of the lip: hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands
Vermilion border: thin keratinised epithelium with tall papillae bringing capillaries close to the surface (red colour)
Inner lip (mucosa): non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium with minor salivary glands
Gingiva and hard palate: keratinised masticatory mucosa bound firmly to bone

images.title: Lip mucosa: stratified squamous epithelium over connective tissue
images.description: Lip section stained with H&E, showing a thick stratified squamous epithelium with ridges pushing down into the underlying connective tissue (lamina propria). The left panel is the raw field and the right panel repeats it with labels added; no magnification is given in the source. Students should find the layers of epithelial cells, the paler connective tissue beneath them, and small blood vessels with red blood cells in that connective tissue.

tissues.name: Tongue & taste buds
tissues.summary: The tongue is a muscular organ whose upper surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium forming papillae, and many of these papillae carry taste buds. Its interlacing skeletal muscle moves food during chewing and swallowing and helps shape speech.
features: Filiform papillae: conical and keratinised, with no taste buds, and the most numerous papillae
Fungiform papillae: mushroom-shaped, with taste buds on the top surface
Circumvallate papillae: large, set in a trench, with taste buds in its walls and serous von Ebner glands at its base
Foliate papillae: folds on the posterolateral margins, with taste buds in their walls
Interlacing skeletal muscle fibres in three planes, cut lengthways and in cross section
Taste buds: pale barrel-shaped clusters of gustatory and supporting cells, opening through a taste pore

images.title: Tongue dorsal surface with labelled tissue layers, H&E
images.description: Annotated H&E-stained section of the dorsal (upper) surface of the tongue, with coloured lines marking epithelium, connective tissue, muscle and a glandular zone. Students should find the epithelial papillae along the top, the connective tissue cores inside them and the interlacing skeletal muscle below. The green glandular label does not clearly match any glands in this field.

images.title: Tongue mucosa with fat cells and gland lobules

The source does not name the stain, and the maroon epithelium with yellow-brown connective tissue is not the colouring of standard H&E. images.source_description: Tongue

images.title: Striated muscle of the tongue with lingual glands, H&E
images.description: H&E-type section of tongue striated muscle, cut in longitudinal and cross section, with purple lingual gland acini lying between the bundles. A duct-like structure runs through the lower middle of the field. Students should separate the long pink fibres from the polygonal cross sections and find the gland acini between the muscle bundles.

images.source_description: Поперечная мышечная ткань языка

images.title: Tongue muscle bundles with lingual gland acini, H&E
images.description: H&E-type section of tongue striated muscle with purple gland acini (lingual salivary glands) lying between the pink muscle bundles. A duct-like profile with a central lumen sits at the lower right of the field. Students should separate the purple acini from the pink fibres and find this duct.
images.author: Molecularu
images.source_description: Поперечная мышечная ткань языка

images.title: Tongue papillae types and taste bud structure, labelled diagram
images.description: Labelled diagram of the upper tongue surface showing fungiform, filiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae, with an inset micrograph of a taste bud in a circumvallate papilla. A separate enlargement of a taste bud labels the taste hairs, taste pore, and basal, gustatory and transitional cells. Students should learn which papillae carry taste buds and where each type sits on the tongue.

images.title: Coronal section of the tongue showing its intrinsic muscles
images.description: Black and white Gray's Anatomy drawing, altered from Krause, of a coronal section through the tongue. It is a gross anatomy drawing rather than a microscope view, and labels the superior and inferior longitudinal muscles, the transverse muscle, the vertical fibres of the genioglossus, the septum, the papillae and the lingual artery. Students should see how the muscle fibres interlace in three planes within the body of the tongue.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Coronal section of tongue, showing intrinsic muscles. (Altered from Krause.)

tissues.name: Tooth
tissues.summary: The tooth is a mineralised organ for cutting and grinding food, built from enamel, dentine and cementum around a vascular pulp. It sits in a bony socket and is anchored there by the periodontal ligament, forming a gomphosis joint.
features: Enamel: highly mineralised and acellular, lost in decalcified sections
Dentine: pale, with fine tubules containing odontoblast processes
Pulp: loose connective tissue with blood vessels and nerves at the centre
Cementum: thin layer on the root surface, pale and acellular in sections
Developing tooth: enamel organ around a dental papilla at the bud, cap and bell stages

images.title: Tooth in unstained ground section showing dentine
images.description: Appears to be an unstained ground section, with a 0.1 mm scale bar and a blue-violet colour in the image. Striated mineralised dentine fills the upper right, and fibrous, cell-rich soft tissue lies beneath it. A student should look for the fine tubular striations in the dentine and the cells along its edge.
images.author: Doc. RNDr. Josef Reischig, CSc.
images.source_description: This image comes from the archive of Josef Reischig and is part of the 384 pictures kindly donated by the authorship heirs under CC BY SA 3.0 license as a part of Wikimedia Czech Republic's GLAM initiative.

images.title: Stages of tooth development from placode to root formation
images.description: A composite figure of five stained micrographs (appears H&E) showing placode, bud, cap, late bell and root stages. Printed labels mark the epithelium and mesenchyme, stellate reticulum, enamel knot, dental papilla, dental follicle, ameloblasts, enamel, dentine, odontoblasts, crown, root, cell rests of Malassez and Hertwig's epithelial root sheath. The figure shows that the crown forms before root formation starts.
images.author: Thesleff, I. and Tummers, M., Tooth organogenesis and regeneration (January 31, 2009), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.37.1, http://www.stembook.org.
images.source_title: Histology of important stages of tooth development.
images.source_description: Note that all early development is directed at creating the crown and only then root formation is initiated. Ameloblasts differentiate from the epithelium and odontoblasts from the mesenchyme and they deposit the matrices of enamel and dentin, respectively. Ameloblasts and enamel are missing on the root which is covered by the softer dentin and cementum. Ep, epithelium; mes, mesenchyme; sr, stellate reticulum; dm; dental mesenchyme; dp, dental papilla; df, dental follicle; ek, enamel knot; erm, epithelial cell rests of malassez; hers, hertwig's epithelial root sheath.

images.title: Tooth bud: enamel organ surrounding the dental papilla
images.description: A stained section of a tooth bud, shown without labels in a round microscope field (appears H&E). The enamel organ is an epithelial bulb with pale, loosely arranged cells between its outer and inner layers, and a dense dental papilla fills its centre. Pink-staining bone trabeculae appear at the edges of the field.

images.title: Tooth bud section with three lettered structures
images.description: The same stained tooth bud section as the unlabelled view, with lines marking A, B and C and no legend. A and B appear to mark the pale stellate reticulum and the dense dental papilla. The unlabelled version is the one kept.
images.author: Author not recorded on Wikimedia Commons (see source page)

images.title: Enamel and dentine boundary in an out-of-focus section
images.description: An unstained, out-of-focus photograph of a tooth section, with enamel appearing at lower left and dentine at upper right, meeting along a bright junction line. The source says enamel lamellae and enamel tufts are visible, but at this focus they are hard to make out. A sharper image of the same region would be more useful for students.

images.title: Developing tooth crown: ameloblasts, enamel, dentine and odontoblasts
images.description: A stained section (appears H&E) of a developing tooth crown at the maturation stage, with printed labels for ameloblasts, enamel, dentine and odontoblasts. The ameloblasts line the outer face of the forming enamel, and the odontoblasts line the inner edge of the dentine. Students should find the enamel and dentine as pink bands between these two cell layers.

Histology of developing tooth with enamel, dentin, ameloblasts, and odontoblasts labeled. Tooth bud is in maturation/crown stage.

images.title: Developing tooth at the cap stage: enamel organ and dental papilla
images.description: A stained section (appears H&E) of a developing tooth at the cap stage, shown with no labels. An epithelial enamel organ forms a cap over a dense cellular dental papilla, with pale stellate reticulum between them. Students should be able to tell the dense papilla apart from the surrounding loose mesenchyme.

images.title: Tooth enamel surface in a scanning electron microscope
images.description: A scanning electron micrograph, with no stain, which the source describes as tooth enamel. At the magnification shown on the image (148x, 1 mm scale bar) the fractured surface looks cracked and terraced, and no individual enamel prisms are resolved. It shows surface fracture and layering rather than a stained section.

images.source_description: Tooth enamel

images.title: Late bell stage tooth germ in a stained section
images.description: A stained section (appears H&E) of a tooth germ at the late bell stage, shown with no labels, as the source describes. A bell-shaped inner epithelium encloses a dense, cellular dental papilla, and the tissue around the germ is loose mesenchyme. Students should find the epithelial wall and the papilla it encloses.
images.author: No machine-readable author provided. Dozenist assumed (based on copyright claims).

tissues.name: Parotid gland
tissues.summary: The parotid gland is a purely serous salivary gland that secretes watery, amylase-rich saliva through a branching duct system into the mouth.
features: Serous acini with basal basophilia and apical zymogen granules
Prominent intercalated and striated ducts between the acini
Connective tissue septa dividing the gland into lobules
Adipocytes that increase in number with age
Facial nerve branches running through the gland

images.title: Parotid gland: duct and serous acini in H&E section
images.description: Parotid gland in a section that appears to be H&E stained; the source gives no magnification. Duct profiles with pale lumens and a cuboidal to columnar lining sit in loose connective tissue on the left, while the closely packed serous acini on the right have granular, pink-purple cytoplasm and round nuclei. Students should compare the paler ducts with the denser acini and note the fibrous connective tissue separating them.
images.author: Wbensmith
images.source_description: Stratified cuboidal/columnar epithelium is visible in a duct surrounded by connective tissue in the parotid gland

images.title: Salivary gland: glandular profiles with pale lumens, eyepiece photo
images.description: Circular microscope field photographed through the eyepiece, with a pink-purple stain that looks like H&E; the source gives only 'salivary gland' and no magnification. Several pale lumens are surrounded by cells with round nuclei, but the field is soft and vignetted at the edges, so acinar and ductal profiles cannot be told apart with confidence. Students should look for the glandular lumens and nuclei here rather than fine cellular detail.
images.author: Нужина Дарья
images.source_description: salivary gland

tissues.name: Submandibular gland
tissues.summary: The submandibular gland is a paired major salivary gland beneath the floor of the mouth, and its mixed secretion, mostly serous, drains into the mouth through the submandibular (Wharton's) duct. Its secretory units are mainly serous acini with some mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes, and long striated ducts modify the saliva as it passes along them.
features: Serous acini: rounded clusters of cells with basophilic (purple-staining) cytoplasm
Mucous acini and tubules: pale, clear-staining cytoplasm
Serous demilunes: crescent-shaped caps of serous cells over mucous units (the caps can be partly a fixation artefact)
Long striated ducts with fine basal striations running through the lobules
Fat-rich connective tissue between lobules, with ducts and blood vessels

images.title: Submandibular gland: clusters of secretory acini in a stained section
images.description: Stained section of submandibular gland showing many rounded clusters of secretory acini, each with round nuclei near the base of the cells, separated by thin strands of connective tissue. The stain appears to be H&E, and the source gives no magnification. Students should pick out individual acini and the loose connective tissue that separates the lobules.
images.author: Rollroboter
images.source_description: Mikroskopisches Schnittbild dert Glandula submanibularis

images.title: Submandibular gland: mixed mucous and serous acini with a duct
images.description: H&E-type stained section of submandibular gland, as far as can be judged, showing lobules of mixed secretory acini. Pale mucous acini sit beside darker serous acini, and fibrous connective tissue separates the lobules. A duct with a central lumen lies in the connective tissue at the lower centre, and fat cells are at the upper right; the source gives no magnification.
images.author: Wbensmith
images.source_description: Large ducts are stratified and surrounded by connective tissue. Mucus cell are identifiable by the lack of color in their cytoplasm, while serosal cells have a basophilic color

images.title: Submandibular gland: serous demilunes on mucous acini, eyepiece view
images.description: Photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece of a circular field of submandibular gland, with a strong blue vignette and a dark probe crossing the lower field. Pale mucous acini are visible, and darker pink serous cells appear as crescent-shaped caps over some of them; these are the serous demilunes, named in the source after Giannuzzi. The stain appears to be H&E, and the source gives no magnification.
images.author: Anara111111
images.source_description: Histology of submandibular glands

images.title: Myoepithelial cells around acini, alpha-smooth muscle actin stain
images.description: Immunohistochemistry for alpha-smooth muscle actin, shown as brown staining with a blue nuclear counterstain, highlighting myoepithelial cells (arrows) that wrap round secretory acini. The source describes a strong positive reaction and gives a 20 micrometre scale bar, but it does not name the organ. Students should look for the flattened brown cells on the outside of the acini, which contract to push secretion out.
images.author: El Sadik A., Mohamed E., El Zainy A.
images.source_description:
Células mioepiteliales (flechas), que rodean los acinos glandulares.

Reacción de αSMA positiva fuerte.

Barra de escala= 20 μm

images.title: Submandibular gland: serous and mucous acini, textbook diagram
images.description: Engraved textbook drawing of a human submaxillary (submandibular) gland, credited to R. Heidenhain, showing lobules in section. The caption places the mucous alveoli on the right and the serous alveoli on the left, and the drawing matches this: the stippled, dark units on the left are serous, while the pale, clear units on the right are mucous. It is a line drawing, so no stain or magnification applies, and the fibrous septa outlining each lobule are clearly drawn.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Human submaxillary gland. (R. Heidenhain.) At the right is a group of mucous alveoli, at the left a group of serous alveoli.

tissues.name: Sublingual gland
tissues.summary: The sublingual gland is a mixed salivary gland beneath the tongue in the floor of the mouth, producing mainly viscous mucous saliva that lubricates the oral cavity. Its acini are dominated by pale mucous cells, with only a few serous demilunes, and its ducts are short and hard to see.
features: Mostly mucous acini with pale, foamy cytoplasm and flattened basal nuclei
Few serous demilunes capping some mucous acini
Short, inconspicuous striated ducts
Lobules separated by thin connective tissue septa carrying ducts and vessels

tissues.name: Oesophagus
tissues.summary: The oesophagus is a muscular tube that carries food from the pharynx to the stomach. Its wall has a thick, non-keratinised stratified squamous lining, submucosal mucous glands, and a muscle coat that changes from skeletal muscle at the top to smooth muscle at the bottom.
features: Thick non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, with nuclei still visible in the surface cells
Lamina propria papillae pushing up into the epithelium
Submucosal mucous glands with pale acini and ducts
Muscularis externa: skeletal muscle in the upper third, smooth muscle in the lower third
Adventitia (loose connective tissue) rather than serosa in the chest part
Lymphoid aggregates in the lamina propria and submucosa

images.title: Stratified squamous epithelium in a normal oesophageal biopsy (H&E)
images.description: A normal oesophageal biopsy stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), cut across the lining. Several layers of cells are stacked on the surface, with dark, crowded basal cells along the lower edge and flatter, paler cells near the top. The source gives no magnification; students should look for the layering and the small nuclei that remain in the surface cells.
images.author: Samir@enwiki
images.source_description: H&E stain of normal biopsy of esophagus showing stratified squamous cell epithelium.

images.title: Oesophageal lining fold with submucosal glands (eyepiece photo)
images.description: A photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece of a section of the oesophageal wall in a pink and purple stain, probably H&E; the source gives no magnification. A fold of lining epithelium borders a pale space, and the loose connective tissue on the right holds rounded gland acini. The image is soft and has a colour cast, so the cell detail is limited.
images.author: Abdulrazakca
images.source_description: Systemic Slide

images.title: Non-keratinised squamous epithelium and lamina propria at 100x (H&E, labelled)
images.description: H&E section at 100x with the source's numbered key: the bracket labelled 2 spans the non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, and the bracket labelled 3 marks the lamina propria beneath it. Arrows point to a lymphocyte, epithelial cells and a fibroblast, and the lowest bracket marks dense irregular connective tissue. Students should identify the epithelial layers and how the cell shapes change from the base towards the surface.

images.title: Oesophageal wall at 20x: mucosa, submucosa and glands (H&E, labelled)
images.description: H&E section at 20x with the source's numbered key, showing the wall of the oesophagus around a central lumen. The mucosa is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium over its lamina propria, while the submucosa holds blood vessels, an excretory duct, mucous glands and a lymphoid aggregate. Students should trace the lining from the lumen out to the submucosa and name each layer.

images.description: H&E section at 400x with four numbered arrows from the source key: epithelial cells with oval nuclei, a lymphocyte with a small dark nucleus, a fibroblast with an elongated nucleus, and the extracellular matrix of the connective tissue. images.title: Oesophageal mucosa, submucosa and lymphoid nodule at 40x (H&E)
images.description: H&E section at 40x with the source's numbered key, showing the mucosa along the top edge, with non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium over lamina propria, and a lymphoid nodule in the submucosa. A blood vessel, an excretory duct and mucous glands lie in the submucosa below it. Students should compare the thick lining with the loose connective tissue and glands beneath it.
