images.title: Schematic cross-section of the oesophageal wall (diagram)
images.description: A schematic cross-section of the oesophageal wall drawn as a circle, with a folded lining along the top. It shows the stratified squamous lining, submucosal glands and blood vessels, a band of muscle, and an outer layer of connective tissue. Arrows point to these parts, but the text labels are cut off at the edge, so students must name them.
images.author: DrJanaOfficial
images.source_description: Schematic diagram of histology of Esophagus

images.title: Oesophageal wall at low power from an eyepiece photo
images.description: A low-power photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece with a phone camera, showing a section of the oesophageal wall in a pink and purple stain, probably H&E; the source gives no magnification. A thin squamous lining runs along the top edge, with clusters of gland acini in loose connective tissue beneath it and a dense pink band, probably muscle, at the bottom. The image is soft and has glare, so only the broad layers can be seen.
images.author: Pavan Chandh Guptha .P
images.source_description: Oesophagus is a hollow , muscular tube that carries food and liquid from your throat to your stomach.

images.title: Trachea and oesophagus in lung tissue at low power (H&E)
images.description: H&E section at low power, as the source states, showing the trachea and oesophagus with the surrounding lung. The lung appears as pale air spaces with thin walls, and a round vessel full of red blood cells sits near the tubes. The wall detail is too coarse to pick out clearly, so students should use this image for the position of the tubes rather than their layers.
images.author: Otávio Astor Vaz Costa
images.source_title: Trachea and esophagus seen from a histological section
images.source_description: Traqueia e esôfago vistos em corte histológico, ao microscópio óptico, corados com HE

images.title: Lining epithelium and lamina propria of the oesophageal wall
images.description: A section of the oesophageal wall in a pink and purple stain, probably H&E, focused on the lining epithelium (lamina epithelialis) and the underlying lamina propria as the source describes. The lining forms thick layers of cells, with a pale gap beside it that is probably the lumen, and the lamina propria at the upper left is loose connective tissue with small blood vessels. The source gives no magnification, so students should look at the layering rather than the cell detail.
images.author: Димитър Митев
images.source_description: Histologic specimen of esophagial wall. The focus is on lamina epithelialis and lamina propria.

images.title: Submucosal mucous glands and a duct in the oesophagus
images.description: A microscope photograph in a pink and purple stain, probably H&E, showing the submucosa; the source gives no magnification. Clusters of mucous gland acini fill most of the field, with dark nuclei pressed against the edge of each acinus, and a small duct with a pale centre sits in the middle. Smooth muscle with elongated nuclei lies at the top left, so students can compare the gland clusters with the muscle layer.
images.author: Iceclanl
images.source_title: Human Esophagus, CS Lower Region Connecticut Valley Southampton, Mass. USA c
images.source_description: Histological Microscope Slide

images.title: Submucosal mucous glands and a duct (second photograph)
images.description: A second photograph of the same field as the previous image, in a pink and purple stain, probably H&E, showing the same mucous gland acini, central duct and smooth muscle at the top left. The colour balance differs slightly, but the content is the same, so it should not be shown alongside the other copy.
images.author: Iceclanl
images.source_title: Human Esophagus, CS Lower Region Connecticut Valley Southampton, Mass. USA d
images.source_description: Histological Microscope Slide

images.title: Oesophageal wall in trichrome stain: epithelium, collagen and muscle
images.description: A transverse section in a trichrome-type stain, which appears to colour collagen blue and muscle and epithelium red; the source gives no magnification. The orange-red stratified epithelium forms a wavy lining along the top, with blue collagen-rich connective tissue beneath it and red muscle bundles with pale rounded areas at the lower right. Students should compare the blue connective tissue layer with the red muscle.
images.author: Lorenzo Apolloni
images.source_title: Trasversal histologic section of human esophagus
images.source_description: Trasversal section of human esophagus

images.title: Blurred orange-red tissue, probably muscle and connective tissue
images.description: A blurred, orange-red stained photograph showing fibrous bundles split by pale clefts, a greyish fibrous area on the left, and pale rounded spaces on the right. The source describes high-power non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, but no such lining is clearly visible here. The image is too soft to confirm the tissue, so it is not reliable for teaching.
images.author: Photograper09
images.source_description: A high-magnification microscope image showing non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The tissue clearly displays multiple layers of cells, which flatten towards the surface, and crucially, the surface cells retain their nuclei, indicating it is a moist, non-keratinized lining.

images.title: Oesophagus wall in transverse section: labelled drawing
images.description: An engraved line drawing of a transverse section of the human oesophagus, made from a drawing by V. Horsley and shown at moderate magnification, as stated in the source. Letters mark the fibrous covering (a), the longitudinal and transverse muscle coats (b and c), the submucous or areolar layer (d), the muscularis mucosae (e), the mucosa with a lymphoid nodule (f) and the stratified epithelium (g). It is an accurate diagram of the oesophagus wall, where the areolar layer is only one labelled part, so it does not depict loose connective tissue on its own.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Section of the human esophagus. (From a drawing by V. Horsley.) Moderately magnified. The section is transverse and from near the middle of the gullet. a. Fibrous covering. b. Divided fibers of longitudinal muscular coat. c. Transverse muscular fibers. d. Submucous or areolar layer. e. Muscularis mucosæ. f. Mucous membrane, with vessels and part of a lymphoid nodule. g. Stratified epithelial lining. h. Mucous gland. i. Gland duct. m’. Striated muscular fibers cut across.

tissues.name: Gastro-oesophageal junction
tissues.summary: The gastro-oesophageal junction is the transition zone where the non-keratinised squamous lining of the oesophagus meets the columnar mucosa of the stomach, marked by the Z-line. The cardiac mucosa just inside the stomach holds coiled glands that secrete mucus.
features: Sharp Z-line where the squamous lining of the oesophagus meets columnar gastric mucosa
Cardiac glands: coiled, mucus-secreting tubular glands in the proximal stomach mucosa
Goblet cells above the junction: intestinal metaplasia, as in Barrett oesophagus
Muscularis mucosae forming the smooth muscle layer beneath the glands

images.title: Cardiac region of the stomach: cardiac glands and their ducts in section
images.description: Historical engraving from Gray's Anatomy showing a section of human stomach mucous membrane near the cardiac orifice, drawn by v. Ebner after J. Schaffer at x45 magnification. The stain is not stated, as it is a drawn engraving rather than a photomicrograph. Students should find the folded mucosa, the coiled cardiac glands and their ducts, a gland with goblet cells similar to intestinal glands, and the muscularis mucosae at the base.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Section of mucous membrane of human stomach, near the cardiac orifice. (v. Ebner, after J. Schaffer.) X 45. c. Cardiac glands. d. Their ducts. cr. Gland similar to the intestinal glands, with goblet cells. mm. Mucous membrane. m. Muscularis mucosæ. m’. Muscular tissue within the mucous membrane.

tissues.name: Stomach (fundus & body)
tissues.summary: The stomach's inner lining (gastric mucosa) of the fundus and body is built from shallow gastric pits and long oxyntic glands. Its parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and its chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which starts protein digestion.
features: Surface mucous cells: simple columnar epithelium lining the shallow gastric pits, with no goblet cells
Oxyntic glands: long tubular glands below the pits in the fundus and body
Parietal cells: large, round, pink (eosinophilic) cells with a central round nucleus, mainly in the middle and upper glands
Chief cells: purple (basophilic) cells with dark nuclei, clustered at the bases of the glands
Muscularis externa: three muscle layers, with an inner oblique layer, seen in the wall at low power

images.title: Chief cell of the gastric gland, electron micrograph
images.description: Electron micrograph of a chief cell from the body (corpus) of the gastric mucosa, so no stain applies, with a 2 µm scale bar. The well-developed Golgi apparatus lies above the nucleus, and many secretory granules of varying size and density fill the supranuclear cytoplasm, with the gland lumen at the upper left. A student should find the bipolar cell organisation, its Golgi and the dense granules packed above the nucleus.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska , Bogdan Lewczuk , Wojciech Petryński , Katarzyna Palkowska , Magdalena Prusik , Krystyna Targońska , Zygmunt Giżejewski , Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz.
images.source_description:
Figura 11. Ultraestructura de las células principales de la glándula gástrica propia de la capa mucosa del "corpus".
A) Organización bipolar de célula principal. Obsérvese el aparato de Golgi (AG) bien desarrollado. Numerosos gránulos secretores, que varían en tamaño y densidad electrónica, ubicados en el citoplasma supranuclear. L: luz de la glándula.

images.title: Neck of a gastric gland with mucous, parietal and chief cells
images.description: Electron micrograph of the neck of a gastric gland in the body of the stomach, with a 5 µm scale bar and no stain. Mucous neck cells (M) lie at the top left, a parietal cell (P) is on the right, and a chief cell (C) lies lower down, with the gland lumen (L) near the centre. Arrows mark bipartite secretory granules in the mucous neck cells, and the asterisk marks stacks of rough endoplasmic reticulum in the chief cell.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska , Bogdan Lewczuk , Wojciech Petryński , Katarzyna Palkowska , Magdalena Prusik , Krystyna Targońska , Zygmunt Giżejewski , Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz.
images.source_description:
Figura 10. Ultraestructura del cuello de una glándula gástrica propia en el cuerpo del estómago.
M= Células mucosas del cuello, P= célula parietal, y C= célula principal (chief) que rodean la L= luz de la glándula. 
Obsérvense los gránulos secretores bipartitos (flechas) y 
el aparato de Golgi bien desarrollado (AG) presentes en las células mucosas del cuello, así como
 las numerosas cisternas del retículo endoplásmico rugoso (asterisco) y 
 los gránulos secretores redondos, densos en electrones (flechas dobles) en las células principales.

images.title: Human gastric glands with parietal and chief cells, light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph of human gastric glands, photographed through a microscope with a digital camera, with no magnification given. The stain appears to be H&E: large pink parietal cells with round central nuclei sit among purple chief cells in the glands, and loose connective tissue with small nuclei lies between them. A student should find the pink parietal cells and the purple chief cells, and tell them apart by cytoplasm colour and nucleus appearance.
images.author: Jpogi at English Wikipedia
images.source_description:
Author's own picture.
A digital camera shot through a microscope; with a human parietal cell glass slide

images.title: Parietal cell beside chief cells, close-up light micrograph
images.description: Close-up light micrograph with an H&E-type pink and purple stain, with no magnification given, and labels reading 'Parietal cell' and 'Chief cells' in the image. The labels mark the large pink cell with a round central nucleus as the parietal cell, and the purple cells with dark nuclei as chief cells. A student should compare the rounded, pink parietal cytoplasm with the darker purple chief cells.

images.title: Stomach fundus wall, low-power H&E section
images.description: Low-power H&E light micrograph of a section through the wall of the stomach, captioned in the source as the bottom (fundus) of the stomach; no magnification is given. The purple mucosa forms one band, a thin pinkish submucosa lies beside it, and the thick muscular coat forms the broad band on the opposite side. A student should identify these three layers of the wall in one view.

images.source_description: Histological preparation. The bottom of the stomach. Stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin

images.title: Normal gastric mucosa at intermediate magnification, H&E
images.description: Intermediate-magnification H&E light micrograph of normal gastric mucosa, the innermost layer of the stomach, as stated in the source. Surface mucous cells line the gastric pits at the top of the field, and the glands below contain pink parietal cells and purple chief cells, with loose lamina propria between the glands. A student should find the pits, the surface lining and the parietal and chief cells in the glands.
images.author: Nephron
images.source_description: Intermediate magnification micrograph of normal gastric mucosa, i.e. inner most layer of the stomach. H&E stain.

images.title: Pyloric region of the stomach wall, light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph photographed through a microscope eyepiece, captioned in the source as the pyloric part of the stomach, with no magnification given and the stain not stated (the pink-red colour suggests an eosin-based stain). The mucosa with its gastric pits forms the top of the field, a band of connective tissue with small vessels (submucosa) lies below, and the thick muscular coat fills the bottom. A student should identify these three layers and the pits in the mucosa, although the blur and circular field make fine detail hard to see.

images.source_description: stomach( histology)

images.title: Parietal cell in a gastric gland neck, electron micrograph
images.description: Electron micrograph of a parietal cell (marked P) in a longitudinal section through the neck of a gastric gland, with no stain and no scale bar shown. The round nucleus sits at the top, and the cytoplasm is packed with mitochondria around branching intracellular canaliculi, which appear as channel-like profiles. A student should find the canaliculi and the mitochondria-rich cytoplasm that mark an acid-secreting parietal cell.

images.description: Electron micrograph of a parietal cell (labelled D) at low magnification, with a 2 µm scale bar and no stain. The source describes a well-developed tubulovesicular system, which appears here as a pale, membrane-rich cluster of tubules and vesicles in the cytoplasm, with the round nucleus below it. A student should find this pale network set among the dense mitochondria.

images.title: Gastric glands of the stomach body in a beaver, light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph of the body region of a beaver stomach, as captioned in the source, with the stain appearing to be H&E and no magnification given. Pink parietal cells with round central nuclei lie among purple-staining chief cells, and small dark nuclei of connective tissue lie between the glands. Because this is beaver tissue, a student should compare the cell arrangement with human material rather than treat it as human.

images.title: Resting parietal cell from a rat, electron micrograph
images.description: Small electron micrograph of a resting parietal cell from a rat, treated with cimetidine and prepared by high-pressure freezing, with a 2 µm scale bar given in the source. The source describes narrow intracellular canaliculi and numerous tubules and vesicles in the cytoplasm, but at this small size these are hard to resolve, and the central nucleus is the main clear feature. The low resolution makes it of limited use for showing fine structure.

images.title: Parietal and chief cells in gastric glands, H&E light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph of gastric glands stained with H&E, with no magnification given, and a dark pointer object in the lower centre of the field. Pink parietal cells with round central nuclei sit among purple chief cells with dark nuclei, and the connective tissue between the glands carries small nuclei. A student should compare the pink parietal cells with the purple chief cells in the same gland.
images.author: en:User:Jpogi
images.source_description: Chief_cells

images.title: Schematic of acid secretion by a parietal cell
images.description: Schematic diagram of a parietal cell showing acid secretion, not a micrograph. It shows CO2 and water forming carbonic acid, with H+ pumped into the stomach lumen by the proton pump (the step that proton pump inhibitors block), HCO3- leaving on the blood side in exchange for Cl-, and K+ and Na+ moved by the pumps on the basolateral side. Students should trace the H+ and Cl- routes from the cell into the lumen and the HCO3- route to the blood.
images.author: MustafaSalahalden
images.source_description:
Parietal cells (also known as oxyntic cells) are epithelial cells in the stomach that secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor. These cells are located in the gastric glands found in the lining of the fundus and body regions of the stomach. 
Proton pump inhibitors are medications that work on the parietal cells in the stomach 
PPIs irreversibly inhibit gastric hydrogen potassium ATPase (H+/K+) ATPase Which is the final step of acid secretion in the stomach

Proton pump inhibitors are explained in this video on youtube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8bJfYbY1E34

tissues.name: Pyloric antrum
tissues.summary: The pyloric antrum is the distal part of the stomach, lined by mucus-secreting mucosa with deep gastric pits and short, coiled mucous glands. Its G cells secrete gastrin, which drives acid secretion, and a thickened circular muscle forms the pyloric sphincter that guards the duodenum.
features: Deep gastric pits, roughly half the mucosal depth
Short, coiled, branched mucous glands with pale mucus-filled cells
G cells (gastrin-secreting) at the gland bases, best shown by gastrin immunostaining
No parietal or chief cells in the glands, unlike the fundus
Thick circular muscle layer forming the pyloric sphincter

images.title: Antral gastric mucosa: surface pits and deep coiled mucous glands
images.description: Section through antral gastric mucosa, H&E stained at 10x, with a 40x inset in the lower right. The surface is lined by tall columnar cells forming deep pits, and the coiled glands below are filled with pale mucus-secreting cells. In the inset, look for pale cytoplasm with flattened basal nuclei, which is typical of mucous cells.
images.author: Carrasco G, Corvalan AH
images.source_description: Histology of normal antral mucosa. H&E 10x; square 40x. Fundic glands are simple, branched tubular glands that extend from the bottom of the gastric pits to the muscularis mucosae; the more distinctive cells are parietal cells.

tissues.name: Duodenum
tissues.summary: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, where chyme from the stomach is mixed with bile and pancreatic juice. Its diagnostic microscopic feature is the Brunner glands in the submucosa, which secrete alkaline mucus.
features: Leaf-shaped villi with crypts of Lieberkühn at their bases
Brunner glands in the submucosa, mucus-secreting clusters that mark the duodenum
Goblet cells in the villus epithelium, stained magenta with PAS
Tall columnar absorptive cells with a brush border lining the villi
Coeliac disease changes: flattened villi, crypt hyperplasia and raised intraepithelial lymphocytes

images.title: Duodenal villi and crypts, H&E high power
images.description: Several leaf-shaped villi of the duodenal mucosa in section, stained with H&E at high magnification. Look for the tall columnar epithelium with a pink brush border, the pale lamina propria with lymphocytes at the core of each villus, and round crypts of Lieberkühn at the base on the right.

images.source_description: Duodenal biopsy showing normal mucosa. H&E stain.

images.title: Duodenal villi and crypts, H&E intermediate power

images.title: Whole duodenal wall in cross section, H&E low power
images.description: Low-power view of a circular section through the duodenal wall, with villi projecting around the outside and a pink ring of muscle inside them. The pale tubular glands at the lower right, in the submucosa, are probably the Brunner glands, which are the diagnostic feature of the duodenum. Stained with H&E.

images.title: Duodenal villi at very high power, H&E

tissues.name: Jejunum
tissues.summary: The jejunum is the middle section of the small intestine and its main absorptive region. Its mucosa forms tall villi on prominent circular folds, which greatly increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients.
features: Tall finger-like villi on high circular folds (plicae circulares)
Columnar enterocytes with a brush border of microvilli
Goblet cells, and Paneth cells with red granules at the crypt bases
Lacteals in the villus cores, which absorb dietary fat
Few Peyer patches and no Brunner glands in the submucosa, which separates it from the duodenum

Thick smooth muscle lies at the top, a loose connective tissue layer with blood vessels runs across the middle (submucosa), and crypts sit at the bottom. images.source_description: Histologic sample of intestine, three tissues are shown.

images.title: Intestinal mucosa with long villi projecting into a lumen
images.description: Microscope photograph of intestinal mucosa with long, narrow villi projecting into a pale lumen at the upper left. images.source_description: Intestine Wall

images.title: Intestinal lining with villi and glands, photographed through an eyepiece
images.description: A phone photograph through a microscope eyepiece of a pink-stained section, with no magnification given. The field shows finger-like villi along the top and many round gland profiles (crypts) below, which looks like the mucosa of the small intestine rather than smooth muscle. tissues.name: Ileum
tissues.summary: The ileum is the final part of the small intestine, lying between the jejunum and the caecum. It absorbs bile acids and vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor, and its wall carries Peyer's patches that sample luminal antigens for the immune system.
features: Peyer's patches: aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa, with no villi over them
M cells: thin epithelial cells with few microvilli over the follicles, sampling luminal antigens
Goblet cells: numerous pale, mucus-filled cells among the columnar epithelium
Shorter villi than the jejunum, with crypts of Lieberkühn at their bases
Brush border of tall columnar absorptive cells lining each villus

images.title: Ileum biopsy: Peyer's patch with lymphoid follicles, intermediate power
images.description: Biopsy of the terminal ileum at intermediate magnification, H&E stain, showing normal histology and a Peyer's patch with two secondary lymphoid follicles. The lymphoid tissue fills most of the field, with villi along the top edge and crypts of Lieberkühn at the bottom. Students should find the dense purple follicle and compare it with the villi and crypts around it.
images.author: CoRus13
images.source_title: Ileum biopsy with lymphoid tissue, intermed. mag
images.source_description: Biopsy of terminal ileum showing normal histology and a lymphoid aggregate of Peyer's patch with two secondary lymphoid follicles. H&E Stain.

images.title: Ileum biopsy: Peyer's patch at low magnification
images.description: Low-power view of a terminal ileum biopsy, H&E stain, showing normal histology and a Peyer's patch with two secondary lymphoid follicles. Several biopsy fragments sit on a white background, with villi and crypts around the large lymphoid aggregate. Students should find the aggregate as a dense purple mass and compare it with the surrounding villi.
images.author: CoRus13
images.source_title: Ileum biopsy with lymphoid tissue, low mag
images.source_description: Biopsy of terminal ileum showing normal histology and a lymphoid aggregate of Peyer's patch with two secondary lymphoid follicles. H&E Stain.

images.title: Ileal villus at high power: columnar cells and goblet cells
images.description: Intestinal villus of the ileum at 100x magnification, as given in the source, with an H&E-like stain that the source does not name. Tall columnar absorptive cells with oval nuclei line the surface, and pale goblet cells lie among them. Eosinophils with red granules are visible in the lamina propria, so students should find the goblet cells and the cells of the lamina propria beneath the epithelium.
images.author: M. Gebauer
images.source_description: Intestinal villus of Ileum (100x magnification)

images.title: Ileum at low power through a microscope, with villi and lymphoid tissue
images.description: Low-power photograph of ileum taken through a microscope eyepiece, with an H&E-like stain that the source does not name and no magnification given. Villi and crypts form the upper mucosa, and dense lymphoid tissue fills the lower part of the field. Students should find the villi, the crypts between them and the lymphoid tissue beneath the mucosa.
images.author: Akula Bhavya Sri
images.source_description: Histology of ileum, last part of small intestine

images.title: Peyer's patch in the ileal wall, low power, with the nodule circled
images.description: Low-power section of the ileal wall in the improved colour version, with a Peyer's patch outlined in red. From left to right the image shows mesenteric fat, villi, the circled submucosal nodules, then the muscle layer and outer covering. The stain looks H&E-like and no magnification is given, so students should find the circled nodule and the villi beside it.
images.author: User:Plainpaper
images.source_description: A picture of Peyer's Patches, which are organized lymphoid nodules commonly found in the small intestines. This histology section was taken from the ileum (NOT jejunum), the final section of the small intestines.

images.title: Ileum section with Peyer's patch nodules under a microscope
images.description: Low-power section of the ileum photographed through a microscope eyepiece, with a probe pointing towards the tissue and an H&E-like stain that the source does not name. Villi and crypts form the upper mucosa, and dense lymphoid nodules of Peyer's patches fill the lower part of the field. Students should find the villi above and the round lymphoid nodules below them.
images.author: Andrjusgeo at Lithuanian Wikipedia
images.source_description: Ileum

images.title: Goblet cells in a mouse ileal villus
images.description: Section through a villus of the mouse ileum, which the source describes as showing mucus-producing goblet cells. An arrow marks a goblet cell at the villus edge, where it shows as a pale, mucus-filled vacuole. The stain is a light pink that the source does not name, and no magnification is given, but the 50 µm scale bar fixes the scale; students should find the goblet cell and the tall columnar cells around it.
images.author: Alfonso Mora
images.source_description: Células caliciformes productoras del moco en el íleon de ratón.

images.title: Ileal villi at 63x magnification
images.description: Section through ileal villi at 63x magnification, as given in the source title, with a pale pink stain that the source does not name. The source describes it as showing the intestinal microvilli, but the brush border is not clearly resolved at this power. Students should find the villi, the columnar epithelium lining them and the lamina propria in the core.
images.author: Alfonso Mora
images.source_description: Corte histológico mostrando las microvellosidades intestinales del íleon.

images.title: Goblet cells in cross-section of intestinal epithelium
images.description: Section through many units of intestinal epithelium (villi or glands) cut across, with pale rounded cells around the rim of each unit that look like goblet cells. The stain appears pink and purple, probably H&E, and the source gives neither a stain nor a magnification. Students should find the goblet cells at the rim and the lamina propria core at the centre of each unit.

tissues.name: Colon & rectum
tissues.summary: The colon, or large intestine, absorbs water and electrolytes and stores and propels faeces, with the rectum as its final segment. Its mucosa has no villi and is lined by straight crypts packed with mucus-secreting goblet cells.
features: No villi: a flat surface with straight, tubular crypts of Lieberkühn
Goblet cells in the crypts and surface, seen as clear mucin-filled vacuoles
Tall absorptive columnar cells with basal nuclei covering the surface
Lamina propria packed with lymphocytes, sometimes forming lymphoid aggregates
Thick muscularis externa, with its longitudinal layer gathered into taeniae coli
Ano-rectal junction, where simple columnar rectal epithelium gives way to stratified squamous anal epithelium

images.title: Colon mucosa at high power: surface cells and goblet-rich crypts
images.description: H&E-stained normal colon at high power, showing the surface and upper crypts. The tall surface cells and the crypt-lining cells contain many clear goblet-cell vacuoles, and the lamina propria between the crypts is packed with lymphocytes. Students should look for the goblet cells in the crypt-lining epithelium.
images.author: CoRus13
images.source_description: Normal histology of the colon. H&E Stain.

images.title: Colon at intermediate power: straight crypts and underlying connective tissue
images.description: H&E-stained normal colon at intermediate power, with the mucosa shown as long straight crypts running down from the surface. A band of pale connective tissue lies beneath the mucosa. Students should trace each crypt from its opening at the surface to its base and look for goblet cells in the crypt lining.
images.author: CoRus13
images.source_description: Normal histology of the colon. H&E Stain.

images.title: Colon wall at low power: mucosa, submucosa and muscle layers
images.description: H&E-stained normal colon at low power, showing much of the wall thickness. Straight crypts make up the mucosa at the top, beneath which a wavy submucosa with small vessels lies above a thick band of smooth muscle. Students should identify these three layers as the main regions of the wall.
images.author: CoRus13
images.source_description: Normal histology of the colon. H&E Stain.

images.title: Colon surface at very high power: columnar cells and goblet cells
images.description: H&E-stained normal colon at very high power, focused on the luminal surface. Tall columnar epithelial cells with elongated nuclei line the surface, and goblet cells appear as clear, round, mucin-filled vacuoles among them. Students should compare these surface cells with the crowded cells of the lamina propria below.
images.author: CoRus13
images.source_description: Normal histology of the colon. H&E Stain.

images.title: Lymphoid aggregate in the colon wall, with crypts around it
images.description: Section of colon showing a large, densely packed lymphoid aggregate in the mucosa, just beneath the surface epithelium, with round crypt profiles around its edge. The aggregate is made of crowded small dark nuclei, most likely lymphocytes, and it appears H&E-stained. Students should find the boundary between the aggregate and the surrounding crypts, and note how the nuclei differ in density from the crypt lining.

images.title: Colon crypts in cross section: evenly spaced, round profiles
images.description: Circular view of normal human colon with crypts cut in cross section, each a ring of cells around a pale lumen. The source describes the crypts as an evenly spaced bed of flowers and notes that the pattern stays regular even in tangential sections. images.source_description: This photo is of the normal human colon. When cut in cross section, the colonic crypts appear like an evenly spaced bed of flowers. Even when maloriented, or tangentially sectioned, the normal colonic mucosa shows an orderly distribution of colonic crypts.

images.title: Annotated ano-rectal junction: rectum meeting the anal canal
images.description: H&E-stained photomicrograph of the ano-rectal junction, with the author's text labels overlaid on the image. tissues.name: Vermiform appendix
tissues.summary: The vermiform appendix is a narrow, blind-ended outpouching of the caecum with colon-type mucosa packed with lymphoid tissue. Its lymphoid follicles make it an immune organ, most prominent in children and young adults.
features: Colon-type mucosa: sparse, irregular crypts with goblet cells and no villi
Large lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa, often with pale germinal centres
Lumen often irregular or star-shaped in cross-section, between thick mucosal folds
Complete outer longitudinal muscle layer, not gathered into bands

images.title: Appendix mucosa with crypts and dense lymphoid tissue
images.description: Eyepiece photograph of a stained section of the vermiform appendix, with an H and E type stain (pink and purple). The source gives no magnification. Students should find the crypts (intestinal glands) set within dense lymphoid tissue, a large lymphoid aggregate in the centre of the field, and paler connective tissue at the upper right.
images.author: Abdulrazakca
images.source_description: Systemic Slide

images.title: Appendix wall with a lymphoid nodule beside mucosal folds
images.description: Eyepiece photograph of a stained section of part of the appendix wall, with an H and E type stain (pink and purple). The source gives no magnification. A round, densely purple lymphoid nodule with a paler centre sits in the middle of the field, with a dark red structure beside it that looks like a congested vessel. Students should find the nodule and the mucosal glands lining the folds at the right edge.
images.author: Jatheesh mohan
images.source_description: Histology of human appendix

images.title: Vermiform appendix in cross-section: lymphoid follicles around the lumen
images.description: Whole cross-section of the vermiform appendix with an H and E type stain, showing the lumen as a star-shaped pale space in the centre. The source gives no magnification. Round lymphoid follicles fill the mucosa and submucosa around the lumen, and the mucosal folds project into it. Students should find the lumen, the ring of lymphoid follicles and the outer wall.
images.author: Andrjusgeo at Lithuanian Wikipedia
images.source_description: Vermiform appendix

images.title: Vermiform appendix in cross-section, blurred low-power view
images.description: Eyepiece photograph of an H and E stained cross-section of the appendix, which the source describes as a low power view. The image is blurred and washed out, so individual cells and glands cannot be made out. The pale star-shaped lumen and the outer wall are the only structures that can be recognised.
images.author: Netha Hussain
images.source_description: Low power view of human appendix H and E staining

tissues.name: Anal canal
tissues.summary: The terminal part of the alimentary canal, running from the rectum to the anal verge. Its lining changes from simple columnar colorectal mucosa, through a transitional zone, to non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium and then keratinised skin at the anal verge, and the internal and external sphincters control continence.
features: Simple columnar colorectal mucosa above the pectinate line, with crypts and goblet cells
Transitional zone around the pectinate line, where columnar and squamous epithelium meet
Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium below the pectinate line
Keratinised skin with hair follicles and apocrine sweat glands at the anal verge
Thick internal sphincter of smooth muscle inside the external sphincter of skeletal muscle
Internal haemorrhoidal venous plexus in the submucosa above the pectinate line

images.title: Coronal section through the anal canal and sphincters
images.description: Line drawing of a coronal section through the anal canal, shown without any stain and with no magnification given. The labelled bladder, ductus deferens and seminal vesicle place it in the pelvis, with the rectum leading down to the anal canal. Students should find the internal sphincter (smooth muscle) lying inside the external sphincter (skeletal muscle), with the levator ani alongside.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Coronal section through the anal canal. (Symington.) B. Cavity of urinary bladder. V.D. Ductus deferens. S.V. Seminal vesicle. R. Second part of rectum. A.C. Anal canal. L.A. Levator ani. I.S. Sphincter ani internus. E.S. Sphincter ani externus.

images.title: Lower rectum and anal wall with dilated haemorrhoidal veins
images.description: Line drawing of the lower rectum and anus, with the mucous membrane removed on one side to show the veins (no stain and no magnification given). The dilated veins pass through the muscular wall to join the external haemorrhoidal plexus, and the internal and external sphincters are labelled beneath them. Students should find the columns and valve of Morgagni and Hilton's white line on the mucosal side, and the change to skin at the anal margin.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Inner wall of the lower end of the rectum and anus. On the right the mucous membrane has been removed to show the dilatation of the veins and how they pass through the muscular wall to anastomose with the external hemorrhoidal plexus. (Luschka.)

tissues.name: Liver
tissues.summary: The liver is the body's main metabolic and detoxifying organ. Hepatocytes form plates between blood-filled sinusoids that run from portal triads to central veins, and they secrete bile into canaliculi that drain towards the portal triads.
features: Classic lobule: central vein with radiating hepatocyte plates
Portal triad: portal venule, hepatic arteriole and bile ductule
Sinusoids lined by fenestrated endothelium and Kupffer cells
Stellate (Ito) cells in the space of Disse, which drive fibrosis in cirrhosis
Zone 3 (around the central vein) is most vulnerable to hypoxia and paracetamol toxicity

images.title: Liver hepatocytes beside fibrous connective tissue
images.description: Liver tissue from a gallbladder resection, stained with H&E; the source gives no magnification. Sheets of hepatocytes with round central nuclei and pale cytoplasm lie below a band of dense pink fibrous connective tissue containing scattered spindle-shaped cells. Students should find the hepatocyte sheets, the fibrous septum and a small vessel with red blood cells at the top left.

images.title: Liver tissue at low power with olive-yellow colouring

images.description: Low-power view of liver with a violet colour and fine brown granules spread through the tissue; the stain is not stated and no magnification is given, but a 0.1 mm scale bar is printed on the image. A large pale vessel lumen lies near the top centre, with smaller pale profiles scattered across the field. Students should identify the hepatocyte plates around these lumens and treat the brown granules with caution, as they may be pigment or stain deposits rather than structure.

images.title: Liver at low power with blue-stained connective tissue
images.description: Low-power view of liver with purple parenchyma and thin blue bands of connective tissue around vessels and along septa. The blue staining suggests a trichrome-type stain, but the stain is not stated and the source gives no magnification. Students should find the portal tracts, where vessel lumens are rimmed by blue connective tissue, and the large vessel at the top left.
images.author: Oktay98
images.source_description: Hepatic tissue aspect with microscope

images.title: Fatty liver: clear lipid vacuoles in hepatocytes
images.description: Low-power view of liver, appearing H&E-stained, with many round clear vacuoles scattered through the hepatocytes, which is consistent with macrovesicular fatty change (steatosis). The source gives no magnification, and lipid is usually dissolved out during processing, so the vacuoles appear as empty holes. Students should find the clear vacuoles and the vessel with a purple wall at the top left.

images.source_description: Hepatic tissue aspect with microscope

images.title: Liver at low power with thin fibrous septa
images.description: Low-power view of liver, appearing H&E-stained, in which thin purple fibrous septa divide the parenchyma into rounded islands. The source gives no description, species, stain or magnification, and the pattern resembles the nodular fibrosis of cirrhosis, but no diagnosis is stated. Students should find the septa and the islands of parenchyma between them.

tissues.name: Gallbladder & bile ducts
tissues.summary: The gallbladder is a muscular sac under the liver that stores bile and concentrates it by absorbing water and salts. Its mucosa is a folded simple columnar epithelium with no goblet cells, lying over a thin smooth muscle wall with no submucosa.
features: Tall simple columnar epithelium with a brush border and no goblet cells
Mucosal folds (rugae) with epithelium covering a loose lamina propria core
No submucosa: lamina propria lies directly on a thin smooth muscle layer
Thin smooth muscle wall with no muscularis mucosae
Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses (chronic cholecystitis): mucosa herniating through the muscle

images.title: Gallbladder wall at intermediate power: mucosa over smooth muscle
images.description: H&E section of a normal gallbladder wall at intermediate magnification. A single layer of tall columnar epithelium lines the mucosa, over loose lamina propria, then bands of smooth muscle, with blood vessels at the lower edge. Students should find the tall lining cells, the smooth muscle fibres with elongated nuclei and the vessels full of red blood cells.
images.author: Nephron
images.source_description: Intermediate magnification micrograph of a normal gallbladder. H&E stain.

images.title: Gallbladder at low power: blurred microscope photograph
images.description: Low-power view of gallbladder wall, taken as a phone photograph through a microscope eyepiece. The stain cannot be confirmed because the whole field is pink, and focus and colour are poor, so the cell layers cannot be resolved. A folded wall with mucosal projections along one edge is only faintly visible, so use it as a rough orientation view only.

images.source_description: Low power view of microscopy of gall bladder

images.title: Gallbladder mucosal folds over smooth muscle, H&E
images.description: Haemalum-eosin (H&E) section of the gallbladder wall, with no magnification given. Branching folds of tall columnar epithelium project into the lumen, each with a loose connective tissue core, and a band of smooth muscle lies below them with blood vessels in the lower stroma. Students should look for the tall lining cells on the folds and the thin muscle layer beneath the mucosa.
images.author: User:Polarlys
images.source_description: gallbladder, haemalum-eosin stain

images.title: Gallbladder epithelial cells absorbing sodium and water (diagram)
images.description: Schematic diagram, not a micrograph, with no stain. It shows two tall epithelial cells joined at their apical ends by a tight junction, with sodium and water moving into the lateral intercellular space, where the fluid becomes hyperosmotic and then flows out as isosmotic fluid into the blood stream. It is a correct teaching diagram of how gallbladder epithelium concentrates bile by absorbing water; note the microvilli on the free surface and the nucleus in each cell.
images.author: Riveromonicadaniela
images.source_description: Histology, Physiology, Cell Biology Illustrations by Monica Rivero Gutierrez

tissues.name: Exocrine pancreas
tissues.summary: The exocrine pancreas is a gland of serous acini that secrete digestive enzymes and bicarbonate-rich fluid into a duct system leading to the duodenum. Scattered among the acini are endocrine islets of Langerhans, which release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
features: Acinar cells in grape-like clusters, with basal basophilia and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules
Centroacinar cells: small, pale cells at the centre of each acinus, where the duct begins
Islets of Langerhans: pale clusters of cells with round nuclei, scattered among the acini
Interlobular connective tissue septa dividing the gland into lobules
No striated ducts (unlike the parotid gland)

images.title: Low-power view of pancreatic lobules

Students should use it to see the lobular pattern of the gland rather than individual cells.

tissues.name: Nasal & olfactory mucosa
tissues.summary: The nasal mucosa lines the nasal cavity, where respiratory epithelium warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air. A patch of olfactory epithelium in the roof of the cavity detects odours.
features: Respiratory region: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Large venous plexuses (swell bodies) in the lamina propria
Olfactory epithelium in the roof: bipolar olfactory neurones, sustentacular and basal cells
Bowman glands beneath the olfactory epithelium, which wash odorants from the surface

images.title: Olfactory region thin section: surface epithelium over connective tissue
images.description: An H&E-stained thin section, 1.5 microns thick according to the source title, shown as a circular microscope field; no magnification is given. The pink surface epithelium is several cells thick and sits on a band of connective tissue with elongated nuclei and an oval duct or vessel profile with a pale lumen. Deeper, a pale zone of rounded cells in lacunae is probably cartilage.

images.title: Nasal mucosa cross-section with surface epithelium and blood vessels
images.description: A cross-section of nasal mucosa stained with a haematoxylin-based stain that looks like H&E, with a 0.1 mm scale bar. A pseudostratified epithelium with fine surface projections (probably cilia) runs along the upper left, above a lamina propria full of cells and vessels, including a thick-walled vessel with red cells in its lumen at the lower centre. Find the surface epithelium, the vessel walls and the thin-walled spaces in the lamina propria.

A thick-walled vessel with red cells in its lumen sits at the upper right. Find the surface epithelium, the glandular acini and the vessel.

images.description: A labelled sagittal diagram of the nasal cavity, not a microscope image, colour-coding its mucosa: squamous at the nostrils (green), respiratory over the turbinates (blue), olfactory in the roof next to the cribriform plate (yellow), and NALT near the tonsils and nasopharynx (red). It shows where each mucosa type lies, which the stained slides cannot show.
images.author: Stella Gänger and Katharina Schindowski
images.source_title: Anatomy of the human nasal cavity
images.source_description: Anatomy of the human nasal cavity. Squamous mucosa (green) is located at the frontal parts of the nasal vestibules. The three turbinates (inferior, middle and superior) humidify and warm the inhaled air. The area covered predominantly with respiratory mucosa is labelled in blue. The olfactory mucosa (yellow) is located next to the cribriform plate at the skull base down to the superior turbinate. Nasally transmitted substances can cross the cribriform plate via different pathways to enter the brain. Nasopharynx-associated lymphatic tissue (NALT) is located in close proximity to the tonsils at the nasopharynx.

Its labels name the epithelium, connective tissue, ethmoid bone and olfactory bulb; no magnification is given. It shows how olfactory axons reach the brain rather than the microscopic structure.

tissues.name: Larynx & vocal folds
tissues.summary: The larynx is a cartilage-supported airway between the pharynx and trachea that protects the lower airway during swallowing and houses the vocal folds that produce voice. Its lining changes from respiratory epithelium in the vestibular folds to non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium over the true vocal folds, which withstands the mechanical stress of vocal fold vibration.
features: True vocal fold: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium over a dense vocal ligament and the vocalis muscle
Reinke space: loose superficial lamina propria under the vocal fold epithelium, which swells in Reinke oedema
Vestibular (false) folds: respiratory epithelium with seromucous glands
Hyaline cartilage of the thyroid, cricoid and arytenoid cartilages
Epiglottis: elastic cartilage core with chondrocytes in lacunae within branching elastic fibres

images.title: Small artery and vein in the epiglottic mucosa, with wall layers labelled
images.description: Transverse section through a small artery and vein in the mucous membrane of a child's epiglottis, shown as a black-and-white line engraving at the magnification given in the source (X 350). The stain is not stated and cannot be judged from the drawing. In the artery (lower), a student should find the lining endothelium (e), the thick circular smooth-muscle media (m) and the outer adventitia (a); the thin-walled vein (upper, V) has a much thinner media.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter
images.source_description: Transverse section through a small artery and vein of the mucous membrane of the epiglottis of a child. X 350. (Klein and Noble Smith.) A. Artery, showing the nucleated endothelium, e, which lines it; the vessel being contracted, the endothelial cells appear very thick. Underneath the endothelium is the wavy elastic lamina. The chief part of the wall of the vessel is occupied by the circular muscle coat m; the rod-shaped nuclei of the muscle cells are well seen. Outside this is a, part of the adventitia. This is composed of bundles of connective tissue fibers, shown in section, with the nuclei of the connective tissue corpuscles. The adventitia gradually merges into the surrounding connective tissue. V. Vein showing a thin endothelial membrane, e, raised accidentally from the intima, which on account of its delicacy is seen as a mere line on the media m. This latter is composed of a few circular unstriped muscle cells a. The adventitia, similar in structure to that of an artery.

tissues.name: Trachea
tissues.summary: The trachea is the cartilage-supported airway that carries air between the larynx and the bronchi, with C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings keeping its lumen open. Its lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, whose cilia move mucus upwards.
features: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells on the luminal surface
Thick basement membrane beneath the epithelium (thickened in asthma)
Seromucous glands in the submucosa
C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, with perichondrium and chondrocytes in lacunae
Trachealis smooth muscle bridging the open back of each C-ring

Labels mark ciliated cells (C), goblet cells (G), basal cells (B) and the basement membrane (BM), which show the layers of the pseudostratified epithelium.

images.description: Low-power H&E section, which the source describes as an elastic artery seen in light microscopy; the stain matches but the content does not. It shows a large lilac plate of hyaline cartilage with scattered chondrocytes, wrapped in a pink perichondrium, with a purple epithelial lining at the right edge. This pattern is more typical of the trachea wall, so the image is misfiled under elastic artery.

tissues.name: Bronchi
tissues.summary: The bronchus is an intrapulmonary airway that carries air between the trachea and the bronchioles. Its wall has a pseudostratified ciliated columnar lining, irregular cartilage plates, spirally arranged smooth muscle and submucosal glands.
features: Irregular plates of hyaline cartilage in the wall, instead of C-shaped rings
Spiral bands of smooth muscle between the mucosa and the cartilage
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Submucosal mucous and serous glands with their ducts
Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue in the mucosa and submucosa
Chronic bronchitis: enlarged submucosal glands (raised Reid index)

images.title: Bronchus with mucous and serous submucosal glands
images.description: H&E-stained section of the bronchial wall (no magnification is given in the source), showing surface respiratory epithelium above loose connective tissue with a glandular duct in the middle of the field. The submucosa is packed with mucous acini, which have pale clear lumens, and serous acini, which are darker and granular; a student should compare these two gland types.
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.source_description: Serous and mucinous bronchial glands, a glandular duct and normal surface respiratory epithelium.

images.title: Cytokeratin 5/6 immunostain of bronchial epithelium: basal cells
images.description: Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin 5/6 on normal bronchial epithelium, with a brown chromogen and a blue counterstain; no magnification is given in the source. The brown staining marks the basal cells at the base of the epithelium, while the cells above are largely unstained and the loose connective tissue beneath is pale.
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.source_description: Positive staining of basal cells of normal bronchial epithelium with CK5-6.

images.title: Cross-section of a secondary bronchus through a microscope eyepiece
images.description: Phone photo taken through a microscope eyepiece of a cross-section of a secondary bronchus, stained pink and purple (probably H&E); no magnification is given in the source. The lumen is largely empty, a black rod crosses the right-hand wall and the image is soft, so the wall layers are hard to tell apart.
images.author: Jpogi at English Wikipedia
images.source_description: Author's own picture. A digital camera shot through a microscope; with a human cross sectional cut of a secondary bronchus

images.title: Bronchial epithelium: ciliated, goblet, basal and club cells
images.description: Labelled schematic of the bronchial lining, not a micrograph, showing pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with ciliated cells (1), goblet cells (2), basal cells (3) and club cells (4). Students should find the cilia on the ciliated cells, the mucin vacuoles of the goblet cells, the small nuclei of the basal cells at the base, and the apical granules of the club cell, which has no cilia.
images.author: John.devos
images.source_description: L'épithélium bronchique est un épithélium cylindrique pseudostratifié cilié qui comprend des cellules ciliées (1), des cellules caliciformes (2), des cellules basales (3) et des cellules club (4)

images.title: Bronchial lining epithelium at high power (eyepiece photo)
images.description: Photo taken through a microscope eyepiece of a thin, pink H&E-stained lining layer, labelled in the source as magnified 600 times. The image is soft and the individual nuclei are hard to make out, so the pseudostratified arrangement is hard to confirm from this image.
images.author: User:Zainubrazvi
images.source_description: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium lining the bronchus (Light Microscope, Hemotoxin and Eosin dye, Magnified 600 times)

tissues.name: Bronchioles
tissues.summary: Bronchioles are the small airways, usually under 1 mm across, that carry air deep into the lung without cartilage or glands. Their wall contains a relatively thick layer of smooth muscle that controls airway calibre, and terminal bronchioles lead on into respiratory bronchioles, where alveoli open and gas exchange begins.
features: No cartilage in the wall, unlike bronchi
No submucosal glands
Relatively thick ring of smooth muscle around the lumen
Ciliated simple columnar epithelium with club (Clara) cells, flattening to cuboidal in terminal bronchioles
Respiratory bronchioles with alveoli opening from their walls

images.title: Respiratory zone diagram (Spanish labels): bronchiole to alveoli
images.description: Labelled illustration of the respiratory zone, with labels in Spanish, showing a terminal bronchiole with smooth muscle in its wall, the respiratory bronchiole, the alveolar duct, the alveolar sac with alveolar pores, and the capillary network around the alveoli. It is a diagram, not a microscope image, so no stain or magnification applies. It shows how the bronchiole feeds into the gas-exchange alveoli.
images.author: OpenStax College
images.source_description: Esquema en el que describe el alveolo pulmonar y la red capilar que hace posible el intercambio de oxígeno entre el alveolo y la sangre.

images.title: Lung histology, H&E: terminal and respiratory bronchioles with alveoli
images.description: Photomicrograph of lung tissue stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), with pointer lines and letters A to D already drawn on it, although the file is titled unlabelled. The source gives A as the respiratory bronchiole, B the alveolar duct, C the alveolar sac and D an alveolus. The Wikimedia title gives 200x, but the source URL names the slide 20X, so the magnification is uncertain. Look for the thick-walled terminal bronchiole at lower left, the respiratory bronchiole, the alveolar duct and sac, and the thin-walled alveoli around them.
images.author: RWhitwam
images.source_description:
Photomicrograph from: https://histologyslides.med.umich.edu/Histology/Respiratory%20System/129_HISTO_20X.htm. Michael Hortsch & the University of Michigan Medical School.
A - respiratory bronchiole.
B - alveolar duct.
C - alveolar sac.

D - alveolus.

images.title: Respiratory zone diagram: terminal bronchiole, alveolar ducts and sacs
images.description: Labelled English-language illustration of the respiratory zone from the Anatomy and Physiology material on the Connexions website. It shows a terminal bronchiole with smooth muscle in its wall, the respiratory bronchiole, the alveolar duct, the alveolar sac with alveolar pores, and the capillaries around the alveoli, with deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery and oxygenated blood to the pulmonary vein. It is a diagram rather than a microscope image, so no stain or magnification applies.
images.author: OpenStax College
images.source_description: Illustration from Anatomy & Physiology, Connexions Web site. http://cnx.org/content/col11496/1.6/, Jun 19, 2013.

tissues.name: Lung alveoli
tissues.summary: The lung alveoli are the millions of thin-walled air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide pass across the air-blood barrier, giving the lungs a gas-exchange surface of roughly 70 m². Their walls are lined mainly by flat type I pneumocytes, while type II cells secrete surfactant.
features: Thin alveolar septa around open air spaces, lined by flat type I pneumocytes (about 95% of the surface)
Cuboidal type II pneumocytes at the corners of alveoli, which secrete surfactant
Capillaries packed with red blood cells within the septa
Alveolar macrophages ('dust cells') in the air spaces, which may be full of haemosiderin in heart failure
Bronchioles with alveoli opening off them, and pores of Kohn joining neighbouring alveoli

images.title: Bronchiole surrounded by alveoli (H&E)
images.description: Normal lung section through a bronchiole, with the alveoli around it. The stain looks like H&E (pink and purple), and the source gives no magnification. Students should find the folded bronchiolar lining, the thin alveolar septa around it and a thick-walled blood vessel at the upper right.
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.source_description: Bronchiole with surrounding alveoli.

images.title: Alveolar septa with capillaries full of red blood cells
images.description: Thin alveolar septa around open air spaces in normal lung, with a stain that appears to be H&E; the source gives no magnification. The capillaries inside the septa are full of red blood cells, and dark nuclei of the lining cells sit along the walls. Students should find the septa, the red-cell-filled capillaries and the air spaces they enclose.
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.source_description: Normal alveoli surrounding a terminal bronchiole.

images.title: Bronchiole with elastic fibres in its wall
images.description: Normal bronchiole shown with an elastic tissue stain, so the elastic fibres in its wall stain dark and look wavy. The source gives no magnification. Students should find the airway lumen, the folded epithelium lining it and the dark elastic fibres around it.
images.author: Yale Rosen from USA
images.source_description: Normal bronchiole. Elastic tissue stain

images.title: Bronchiole and alveolar ducts, annotated with letter labels
images.description: Annotated section of normal lung tissue from patients with hamartochondroma, with an H&E-type stain; no magnification is given. It shows a bronchiole with its lumen, and the alveoli and alveolar ducts around it, and the figure carries arrows and letters (P, M, BT, PB, DA, A, AS) with no key. Students should find the folded bronchiolar lumen, the wall around it and the alveoli beyond.
images.author: Anhenn O et al. (published in BMC Infect Dis, v.4; 2004), modified by Christian2003
images.source_title: Histology of normal lung tissue in patients with hamartochondroma2
images.source_description: Histology of normal lung tissue in patients with hamartochondroma

images.title: Alveolus diagram: capillaries surround the alveolar air
images.description: Labelled diagram of a cross-section through an inflated alveolus, with pulmonary capillaries shown in cross-section in its walls. The labels read that the capillary blood is completely surrounded by alveolar air, and give about 3 litres of alveolar air in all the alveoli together and about 100 ml of blood in all the pulmonary capillaries. Students should find the central air space, the red blood cells in the capillaries and the thin walls between them.
images.author: Cruithne9
images.source_description: A diagrammatic histological cross-section through a portion of lung tissue showing a normally inflated alveolus (at the end of a normal exhalation), and its walls containing the pulmonary capillaries (shown in cross-section). This illustrates how the pulmonary capillary blood is completely surrounded by alveolar air. In a normal human lung all the alveoli together contain about 3 liters of alveolar air. All the pulmonary capillaries contain about 100 ml blood..

images.title: Airway wall diagram: trachea or bronchus, without and with inflammatory cells
images.description: Two-panel diagram of the wall of a trachea or bronchus, labelled for mucus, goblet cells, epithelium, basement membrane, lamina propria, smooth muscle, glands and cartilage. Panel (b) adds mast cells, macrophages, eosinophils and neutrophils to the lamina propria. It is an unstained diagram of the conducting airway, not of the alveoli, so students should not confuse it with alveolar tissue.
images.author: OpenStax College
images.source_description: Illustration from Anatomy & Physiology, Connexions Web site. http://cnx.org/content/col11496/1.6/, Jun 19, 2013.

images.title: Alveolar sac and alveoli in a stained slide
images.description: Photograph through a microscope of a human alveolar sac on a histological slide, with pink and purple staining that looks like H&E; the source gives no magnification. Students should find the open alveolar air spaces and the thin septa between them, with dark nuclei along the walls. A dark object at the lower right is not tissue.
images.author: Jpogi
images.source_description: A histiologic slide of a human alveolar sac. Picture taken with a digital camera thru a microscope.

images.title: Alveolar septa packed with red blood cells
images.description: Lung section with a pink and purple stain that looks like H&E; the source gives no stain or magnification. The thin alveolar septa are crowded with red blood cells, and the alveolar air spaces show as pale gaps between them. Students should find the packed septa and compare them with the open air spaces.
images.author: Sdfhkjdbhoppiozcxzcxvvdvbdfk at Persian Wikipedia
images.source_description: عکس : رضا کلانی

images.title: Blood-air barrier of the alveolar wall: schematic diagram
images.description: Schematic diagram of the blood-air barrier across an alveolar wall. It shows alveolar air on each side, the fluid lining and epithelial cells on the air side, the basement membrane, the endothelial cells, and plasma with red blood cells on the blood side. The diagram is unstained and carries 2 µm and 5 µm dimension labels, and students should be able to name each layer that gases cross.
images.author: Cruithne9
images.source_description: A histological cross-section through an alveolar wall showing the layers through which the gases have to move between the blood plasma and the alveolar air. The dark blue objects are the nuclei of the alveolar type I epithelial cells (or pneumocytes).

images.title: Respiratory zone: labelled alveoli, alveolar duct and sac
images.description: Labelled section of the respiratory zone of lung, with an H&E-type stain (pink and purple); the source gives no magnification. Text labels mark alveoli, an alveolar duct, an alveolar sac, blood vessels and the lumen of a bronchiole. Students should use them to tell the thin alveolar walls from the airway lumen and the vessels.

images.description: Schematic cross-section of a cluster of alveoli, with labels in Spanish for capillary, alveolus, alveolar macrophage, type I and type II pneumocytes and interalveolar septum.
