tissues.name: Kidney cortex & glomerulus
tissues.summary: The renal cortex is the outer zone of the kidney, made up mainly of renal corpuscles and the convoluted parts of the nephron tubules. Here blood is filtered at the glomeruli, and the tubules then reabsorb and secrete substances to form urine.
features: Renal corpuscle: round glomerular capillary tuft inside a pale Bowman's space
Proximal convoluted tubule: eosinophilic cells with a brush border and a fuzzy lumen
Distal convoluted tubule: smaller, paler cells with a clear, open lumen
Macula densa: tall, crowded distal tubule cells at the vascular pole of the glomerulus
Basement membranes: PAS stain outlines the capillary loops and capsule in magenta

images.title: Kidney section in a light micrograph with a strong orange tint
images.description: Light micrograph of kidney tissue with a strong orange tint and dark vignetting around the edge of the field. Round profiles that may be tubule cross-sections or glomeruli are faintly visible, but the detail is too soft to identify structures reliably, and the stain and magnification are not stated.
images.author: Borislav Yanev
images.source_description: Kidney, as seen under a light microscope, Bonn-Rhine-Sieg University of Applied Sciences, Germany

images.title: Kidney section in H&E with glomeruli among tubules
images.description: H&E-stained kidney section photographed through a microscope, so the field is circular and the image is soft. Several renal corpuscles show as round tufts with a clear Bowman's space, surrounded by pink tubule profiles. Students should find the glomeruli first and then compare the surrounding tubules with them.
images.author: علاء
images.source_description: Kidney H&E

images.title: High-power kidney section labelled as juxtaglomerular cells
images.description: Digital camera photo through a microscope at high magnification, with pink cytoplasm and purple nuclei that suggest H&E (the source does not name the stain). Cells with round nuclei line a large clear lumen, and a dark needle-like object crosses the lower centre, but the granular JG cells in an arteriole wall are not clearly identifiable at this resolution.
images.author: Jpogi
images.source_description: Human JG cells. Digital camera shot through a microscope.

images.title: Kidney cortex with two glomeruli in trichrome stain
images.description: Kidney cortex in a green and red trichrome-type stain, probably Masson's although the source does not say, with a 0.1 mm scale bar. Two glomeruli are visible as round capillary tufts inside pale Bowman's spaces, surrounded by tubules with brown-red cytoplasm. Red blood cells fill the capillaries and green connective tissue surrounds the vessels, so students should compare the glomeruli with the tubules around them.
images.author: Doc. RNDr. Josef Reischig, CSc.
images.source_description: This image comes from the archive of Josef Reischig and is part of the 384 pictures kindly donated by the authorship heirs under CC BY SA 3.0 license as a part of Wikimedia Czech Republic's GLAM initiative.

images.title: Kidney cortex with a glomerulus in trichrome stain
images.description: Kidney cortex in a green and red trichrome-type stain, with a 0.1 mm scale bar. A single large glomerulus sits in the centre-left of the field, its capillaries packed with red blood cells and enclosed by a pale Bowman's space. Tubules with brown-red cytoplasm surround it, and a large green-walled blood vessel lies to the upper right.
images.author: Doc. RNDr. Josef Reischig, CSc.
images.source_description: This image comes from the archive of Josef Reischig and is part of the 384 pictures kindly donated by the authorship heirs under CC BY SA 3.0 license as a part of Wikimedia Czech Republic's GLAM initiative.

images.title: Close-up of a glomerulus next to a tubule and artery in trichrome stain
images.description: Close-up of kidney cortex in a green and red trichrome-type stain, with a 50 um scale bar. A glomerular capillary tuft packed with red blood cells lies at the lower left inside a pale Bowman's space, next to a tubule with brown-red cytoplasm at the top. A blood vessel with a thick green wall sits at the upper right, and nuclei are visible throughout.
images.author: Doc. RNDr. Josef Reischig, CSc.
images.source_description: This image comes from the archive of Josef Reischig and is part of the 384 pictures kindly donated by the authorship heirs under CC BY SA 3.0 license as a part of Wikimedia Czech Republic's GLAM initiative.

images.title: Kidney cortex at low power with several glomeruli among tubules
images.description: Author's own digital camera photo of kidney cortex through a microscope, in a pink and purple stain that looks like H&E (the source does not name it). Several renal corpuscles are scattered among the tubules, each a round tuft with a pale Bowman's space. A dark needle-like artefact crosses the centre of the field, and no magnification is given.
images.author: Jpogi at English Wikipedia
images.source_description: Author' own picture. Human Kidney (Cortex). Digital camera shot through a microscope.

images.title: Nephron and collecting duct, labelled diagram
images.description: Colour schematic, not a microscope image, of a nephron and a collecting duct. It shows the glomerulus in Bowman's capsule, the proximal and distal tubules, the loop of Henle, the macula densa and the afferent and efferent arterioles, and its labels are in German. Students should trace the route from the glomerulus through each tubule segment to the collecting duct.
images.author: Calibu28
images.source_description: Die Abbildung zeigt die verschiedenen Abschnitte des Tubulussystems.

images.title: Renal corpuscle in PAS stain showing glomerular capillary loops
images.description: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stained section of one renal corpuscle, with the glomerulus sitting inside Bowman's capsule. PAS colours the basement membranes magenta, so the capsule and capillary loops stand out as a bright skeleton while the surrounding tubules are pale. The source gives no magnification, so students should trace the capillary loops and the urinary space between them and the capsule.
images.author: Ed Uthman (Pathologist), website: [2]
images.source_description:
Renal corpuscle (Glomerulus), Periodic Acid-Schiff Stain (PAS).
The PAS stain lights up basement membranes, so it's very nice for appreciating the skeleton of the glomerulus of the kidney.

images.title: Scanning electron micrograph of fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium
images.description: Scanning electron micrograph of the inner surface of a glomerular capillary at 100,000 times magnification, with a 200 nm scale bar; the German caption reads 'fenestrated endothelium of a glomerular capillary'. The many round to oval holes are fenestrae, the pores that let plasma pass towards the urinary space. As an electron micrograph it shows surface detail that light microscopy cannot resolve.
images.author: SecretDisc
images.source_title: Inner view of fenestrae in capillary of glomerulus in Scanning Electron Microscope, magnification 100,000x
images.source_description: Inner view of fenestrae in capillary of glomerulus in Scanning Electron Microscope, magnification 100,000x

images.title: Diagram of glomerular cell types: mesangial cell, capillaries and podocytes
images.description: Coloured schematic, not microscopy, of the cells in a glomerulus: a central mesangial cell, capillary loops with red blood cells and an endothelial lining, and podocytes with their foot processes around the outside. The source describes it as showing podocytes, endothelial cells and mesangial cells. Students should use it to match each cell type to its position relative to the capillary loops.
images.author: Artwork by Holly Fischer
images.source_description: This image shows the types of cells present in the glomerulus part of a kidney nephron. Podocytes, Endothelial cells, and Glomerular mesangial cell are present.

images.title: Diagram of kidney blood supply through glomeruli, arteries and veins
images.description: Coloured schematic, not microscopy, of kidney blood flow with arteries in red and veins in blue. It shows glomerular capillary tufts fed from a vertical artery and drained to a vertical vein, plus a U-shaped loop of vessels at the bottom that resembles the vasa recta of the medulla. It gives the vascular context for the cortex but does not show cell detail.
images.author: Artwork by Holly Fischer
images.source_description: This image shows the arterial and venous blood flow of the kidney.

images.title: Kidney cortex at low power: glomeruli and renal tubules
images.description: Pink-stained section seen through a microscope eyepiece, appearing to show renal cortex at low power. The source gives no stain or magnification, but the pink colour suggests an eosin-based stain. Several round glomeruli sit among many cut tubule profiles, and the thin parietal layer of Bowman's capsule cannot be resolved at this power, so the image belongs with the kidney cortex tissue.
images.author: Naz Amann
images.source_description: Tissue

tissues.name: Kidney medulla & collecting system
tissues.summary: The kidney medulla is the inner zone of the kidney, made of renal pyramids that contain the loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta. It concentrates urine by building a salt gradient through the interstitium, which draws water out of the collecting ducts.
features: Collecting ducts: cuboidal to columnar cells with distinct borders, around wide lumens (principal and intercalated cells)
Thin limbs of Henle: very thin walls that look like capillaries but contain no red blood cells
Vasa recta: thin-walled capillaries running parallel to the tubules, often with red blood cells in the lumen
Papillary ducts: large, tall columnar ducts that open onto the renal papilla into a minor calyx

images.title: Renal medulla: tubules cut in cross-section
images.description: Renal medulla in a stained microscope section, with many tubules cut in cross-section and separated by a thin interstitium. The section appears to be H&E stained, with purple nuclei and pink cytoplasm. Students should look for the open lumens ringed by cuboidal to low columnar epithelial cells with round central nuclei, and the thin pink interstitium between the tubules.
images.author: Pathologist without beard
images.source_description: Renal medulla under microscope

tissues.name: Ureter
tissues.summary: The ureter is a muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. Its lumen is lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium), and peristaltic smooth muscle in the wall propels the urine onward.
features: Star-shaped lumen: the mucosa is thrown into folds, so the lumen looks stellate in cross-section
Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lining the lumen as a multilayered purple band that follows every fold
Lamina propria: loose connective tissue filling the core of each fold, beneath the epithelium
Thick smooth muscle wall: inner longitudinal and outer circular layers, with an extra outer longitudinal layer lower down
Outer adventitia of loose connective tissue, with fat and small blood vessels around the wall

images.title: Ureter in transverse section: low-power view with labelled wall layers
images.description: Labelled low-power micrograph of a transverse section of the ureter, H&E-stained in pink and purple. The folded mucosa forms a star-shaped lumen surrounded by a thick smooth muscle wall, with loose connective tissue and some fat outside. Students should find the lumen, the mucosal folds, the smooth muscle layer and the adventitia at the edge.
images.author: OpenStax College
images.source_description: Illustration from Anatomy & Physiology, Connexions Web site. http://cnx.org/content/col11496/1.6/, Jun 19, 2013.

images.title: Ureter in transverse section: faint, washed-out low-power view
images.description: Photograph through a microscope of a transverse section of the ureter on a pale slide, with a dark needle lying across the field. The staining is too weak to identify with confidence, so the lumen and mucosal folds are faint. Students can make out the star-shaped lumen, but the wall layers are too pale to tell apart.
images.author: علاء
images.source_description: Ureter slide

images.title: Ureter in transverse section: star-shaped lumen with mucosal folds
images.description: Photomicrograph through a microscope, showing a transverse section of the ureter in a circular field, with a dark needle crossing the lumen. The stain is pink and purple, consistent with H&E. The lumen is star-shaped with several folds of mucosa, while the outer wall is pale and blurred, so students should focus on the lumen shape.
images.author: Netha Hussain
images.source_description: Histology of ureter

images.title: Ureter lumen: urothelial lining and underlying connective tissue, close view
images.description: Close-up photograph taken through a microscope with a digital camera, showing the lumen of the ureter. The lumen is star-shaped and bordered by a thin, dark purple urothelial lining, with pink connective tissue beneath it. The stain appears to be H&E, and students should see the thin lining following each fold.
images.author: Jpogi at English Wikipedia
images.source_description: Author' own picture. Human Ureter. Digital camera shot through a microscope.

images.title: Ureter wall layers in transverse section: labelled line drawing
images.description: Labelled line drawing of a transverse section of the ureter, with the lumen and folded epithelium at the centre and the wall layers around it. The labels mark the epithelium, the connective tissue beneath it, the mucosa as a whole, the muscular layer and the adventitia. The labels are in Portuguese, but the structures match the English drawings.

tissues.name: Urinary bladder
tissues.summary: The urinary bladder is a hollow, distensible reservoir that stores urine until it is voided. Its wall is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) over a lamina propria and a thick detrusor of interlacing smooth muscle, and the lining flattens as the bladder fills.
features: Transitional epithelium (urothelium): stratified lining several cells deep
Umbrella cells: large, often binucleate surface cells that cover the lumen
Lining thins and flattens when distended, and is thick and folded when collapsed
Lamina propria: loose connective tissue with spindle-shaped nuclei beneath the urothelium
Detrusor: thick smooth muscle layer of interlacing bundles cut in several planes

tissues.name: Urethra
tissues.summary: The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body, and in males it also carries semen. Its lining changes along its length, from urothelium (transitional epithelium) near the bladder to stratified squamous epithelium at the external opening.
features: Prostatic urethra: urothelium (transitional epithelium) with rounded surface cells
Membranous and spongy urethra: pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium
Navicular fossa and external opening: stratified squamous epithelium
Mucous glands of Littré opening into the lumen of the spongy urethra
Smooth muscle coat outside the lamina propria; in males the spongy urethra sits in erectile tissue with venous sinusoids

tissues.name: Pancreatic islets of Langerhans
tissues.summary: Islets of Langerhans are small clusters of hormone-secreting endocrine cells scattered through the exocrine pancreas. They release insulin, glucagon, somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide directly into the blood to regulate blood glucose.
features: Pale, rounded clusters of endocrine cells scattered among darker exocrine acini
Islet cells with round nuclei and pale cytoplasm, unlike the granular acinar cells around them
Dense capillary network running between the islet cells
Beta cells (insulin) form most of the islet and lie centrally; alpha cells (glucagon) lie at the periphery, best shown by immunostaining
Type 1 diabetes: lymphocytes infiltrate the islets (insulitis); type 2: amyloid deposits (amylin) form within islets

tissues.name: Pituitary gland
tissues.summary: The pituitary gland is a small endocrine gland at the base of the brain with two main lobes. The glandular anterior lobe (pars distalis) makes GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH, while the neural posterior lobe (pars nervosa) stores and releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.
features: Anterior lobe (pars distalis): cell clusters of acidophils (pink cytoplasm), basophils (purple cytoplasm) and pale chromophobes
Capillaries packed with red blood cells running between the anterior lobe cell clusters
Posterior lobe (pars nervosa): pale, sparsely cellular neural tissue of unmyelinated axons and pituicytes
Herring bodies: swollen axon endings in the posterior lobe that store ADH and oxytocin
Pars intermedia: a thin band of cells between the lobes, sometimes with colloid-filled Rathke cysts

tissues.name: Thyroid gland
tissues.summary: The thyroid gland is an endocrine organ made of closed follicles, each lined by cuboidal cells that make thyroglobulin and store it as colloid, from which the hormones T3 and T4 are released. Parafollicular C cells between the follicles secrete calcitonin.
features: Follicles lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, taller when active and flatter when resting
Pale colloid in the follicle lumen, with scalloped margins and resorption vacuoles at the edge when active
Parafollicular C cells (calcitonin) between follicles, often paler than the follicular cells
Graves disease: tall, hyperplastic follicular cells with scalloped colloid
Hashimoto thyroiditis: dense lymphocytic infiltrate, lymphoid follicles and Hürthle cells

tissues.name: Parathyroid gland
tissues.summary: Parathyroid glands are usually four small endocrine glands on the back of the thyroid. Their chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium levels.
features: Chief cells in cords, nests and sheets, with round nuclei and pale cytoplasm
Rich capillary network between the cell cords, often with red blood cells in the lumen
Oxyphil cells: larger, with pink (eosinophilic) cytoplasm and many mitochondria; increase with age
Clear adipocytes between the cell nests, increasing with age
Fibrous capsule and septa, with larger vessels running through the fibrous tissue

images.title: Parathyroid chief and oxyphil cells with a capillary
images.description: Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) section of the parathyroid gland, showing a dense sheet of chief cells with round, dark nuclei and pale to pinkish cytoplasm. A capillary packed with red blood cells runs through the centre, and the pinker, more eosinophilic cytoplasm at the lower left is typical of oxyphil cells. Students should find the capillary and compare the pale chief cells with the pinker oxyphil cells.

tissues.name: Adrenal (suprarenal) gland
tissues.summary: The adrenal (suprarenal) gland sits on the upper pole of each kidney. Its outer cortex makes steroid hormones in three zones (glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis), and its inner medulla, a modified sympathetic ganglion, makes adrenaline and noradrenaline.
features: Zona glomerulosa: thin outer band of small cell clusters under the capsule (aldosterone)
Zona fasciculata: widest zone, cords of pale, lipid-rich cells (cortisol)
Zona reticularis: branching cords of cells with lipofuscin pigment (androgens)
Medulla: clusters of chromaffin cells around thin-walled sinusoids (adrenaline, noradrenaline)
Central adrenomedullary vein running through the medulla

images.title: Adrenal gland: hand-drawn microscope view with the zones labelled
images.description: A coloured-pencil drawing, in pink and purple, of a circular microscope field through the adrenal gland, with handwritten labels for the capsule, zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis and medulla. No magnification is given, and it is a drawing rather than a photograph. Students should look for the glomerulosa as small clusters under the capsule, the fasciculata as wide cords of pale cells, and the medulla as a looser area at the bottom.

tissues.name: Pineal gland
tissues.summary: The pineal gland is a small endocrine organ in the roof of the diencephalon that secretes melatonin from pinealocytes arranged in lobules. Calcified brain sand (corpora arenacea) accumulates with age and serves as a useful radiological landmark.
features: Pinealocytes in lobules, with round nuclei and pale cytoplasm
Interstitial astrocytes with elongated nuclei in the septa between lobules
Corpora arenacea (brain sand): dark calcified concretions that increase with age
Fibrous septa and a rich capillary bed dividing the lobules
Calcified pineal is a radiological midline landmark on skull X-ray and CT

images.title: Rat pineal gland at embryonic day 21: Pax6 and vimentin immunofluorescence
images.description: Confocal immunofluorescence of a sagittal section through the rat pineal gland at embryonic day 21, with Pax6 nuclei in green and vimentin in red. Panel G1 (20x, 75 µm scale bar) shows the gland as a compact, rounded mass of Pax6-positive cells surrounded by vimentin-rich tissue, while G2 to G4 (60x, 25 µm scale bar) show individual nuclei and vimentin fibres. A student should see that by this stage the gland is a recognisable globular structure.
images.author: María P. Ibañez Rodriguez, Stephen C. Noctor, Estela M. Muñoz
images.source_description:
Figura 1. La glándula pineal se desarrolla a partir de células neuroepiteliales que expresan el factor de transcripción Pax6 y el filamento intermedio vimentina.
Los paneles muestran microscopía confocal de secciones sagitales inmunomarcadas de la glándula pineal de rata (PG) del día embrionario (E) E21.
 La PG está densamente poblado por células que expresan Pax6 (verde). 
 En E21, la PG se ha desarrollado hasta convertirse en una estructura globular reconocible. 
 G₁ 20x; Barra de escala= 75 μm.
 G2-G4= 60x; Barra de escala= 25 μm.

images.title: Vole brain near the pineal gland: interlaced blood vessels, modified azan stain
images.description: Light micrograph of a longitudinal section through the brain of the northern red-backed vole (Clethrionomys (Myodes) rutilus) in the area of the pineal gland, stained with modified azan. Blood vessels show as orange-yellow bands that interlace through the blue-stained brain tissue, so this is a vascular view of the region rather than typical pinealocyte lobules. Students should note the vessel network and treat it as context around the gland.
images.author: Stranger
images.source_description: Longitudinal section of the brain of the northern red-backed vole (Clethrionomys (=Myodes) rutilus) in the area of the pineal gland. Interlacing of blood vessels. Staining with modified azan. Light micrograph.

images.title: Rat pineal gland, embryonic day 15 to 21: Pax6 and vimentin series
images.description: Confocal immunofluorescence series of sagittal sections through the developing rat pineal gland from embryonic day 15 to day 21, with Pax6 in green and vimentin in red, at 20x with a 75 µm scale bar. The gland is a thin, curved band at E15 and E16 that thickens into a rounded mass by E21. Labels mark the third ventricle (3v), posterior commissure (PC) and subcommissural organ (SCO) near the gland, and the series shows how it develops from neuroepithelium.
images.author: María P. Ibañez Rodriguez, Stephen C. Noctor, Estela M. Muñoz
images.source_description:
Figura 1. La glándula pineal se desarrolla a partir de células neuroepiteliales que expresan el factor de transcripción Pax6 y el filamento intermedio vimentina.
Los paneles muestran microscopía confocal de secciones sagitales inmunomarcadas de la glándula pineal de rata (PG) del día embrionario (E) 15 al E21.
Los paneles A1-G1 muestran la expresión de Pax6 (verde) y vimentina (VIM, rojo) en células precursoras pineales a bajo aumento.

tissues.name: Testis
tissues.summary: The testis is the male gonad, where seminiferous tubules produce sperm through spermatogenesis, supported by Sertoli cells. Leydig cells in the interstitial tissue between the tubules secrete testosterone.
features: Seminiferous tubules: round cross-sections with a central lumen, packed closely together
Germ cells in layers: spermatogonia at the base, spermatocytes above, spermatids near the lumen
Sertoli cells: tall supporting cells with large nuclei and a prominent nucleolus, joined by tight junctions (blood-testis barrier)
Leydig cells: clusters in the interstitial tissue between tubules, making testosterone (Reinke crystals on electron microscopy)
Peritubular myoid cells: flattened cells outside the basal lamina of each tubule
Tunica albuginea: thick fibrous capsule around the whole organ

Panel B is a micrograph of one seminiferous tubule that looks H&E stained, with no magnification given, and the figure labels its spermatogonia, primary and secondary spermatocytes, spermatids and Sertoli cells.
images.author: Dusan Zivkovic ass
images.source_title: Morphology of the human testis. A. Cross section of the human testes
images.source_description: Figure 1. Morphology of the human testis. A: Cross-section of the human testes. The organ is divided in lobules, each containing highly coiled seminiferous tubules, eluting its secretions from both ends into the rete testis, which transfers the differentiated germ cells into the efferent ducts of the epididymis. As they travel through the epididymis, the germ cells reach full maturation and are stored in the epididymis. B: Cross-section micrograph of a histological preparation of a seminiferous tubule. The pool stem cells called spermatogonia renews itself by division, while a part of the population begins to differentiate. As they do so, germ cells move towards the middle of the seminiferous tubules, until they are released into the lumen. Throughout the differentiation process, germ cells are immersed in invaginations on the surface of Sertoli cells that serve as support and quality control.

tissues.name: Epididymis
tissues.summary: The epididymis is a highly coiled duct along the back of each testis where sperm mature, gain the ability to swim and fertilise, and are stored until ejaculation. Its lining is pseudostratified epithelium, surrounded by a thin smooth-muscle coat that thickens towards the tail.
features: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with long stereocilia projecting into the lumen
Principal cells, the main cell type, forming most of the tall epithelial lining
Basal cells: small cells resting on the basement membrane, beneath the principal cells
Lumen filled with sperm, seen as dark heads and tails
Thin smooth-muscle layer around each duct, thickening towards the tail

Microvilli line the luminal surface. Students should use it to match each cell type to its appearance in stained sections, and note that the apical blebs on principal cells release epididymosomes.
images.author: Zhou W., De Iuliis GN., Dun MD., Nixon B.
images.source_description:
Figura 1. Estructura regionalizada y distribución esquemática de los principales tipos de células en el epidídimo de ratón.

(C) Las células principales dominan el soma a lo largo de toda la longitud del epidídimo y son particularmente activas en términos de biosíntesis y secreción de proteínas en los segmentos proximales del epidídimo. En este contexto, una vía de secreción apocrina, que presenta la formación y eventual desprendimiento de grandes estructuras en forma de ampollas del margen apical (es decir, ampollas apicales) de las células principales, parece ser un mecanismo secretor dominante que opera en todos los segmentos del epidídimo. Tras la degradación dentro de la luz del epidídimo, las ampollas apicales liberan una población heterogénea de vesículas extracelulares membranosas, denominadas epididimosomas, que se han implicado en la comunicación intracelular con los espermatozoides y las células epiteliales posteriores. 

Aparte de las células principales, las células claras se distribuyen esporádicamente por todo el epitelio de la capa, cuerpo, y segmentos de cauda en la mayoría de las especies estudiadas y son los principales responsables de la absorción selectiva de los componentes luminales y, a la inversa, de la regulación del pH luminal.


Se ha descrito un conjunto de tipos de células adicionales en el epidídimo, que incluyen células basales, células apicales, células halo, células estrechas (solo se encuentran en el segmento inicial y la zona intermedia) y

images.title: Four segments of the mouse epididymis with H&E sections of each
images.description: Panel A is a schematic of the mouse epididymis showing the initial segment, caput, corpus and cauda, and panel B shows a section from each segment that looks H&E-stained, with no magnification given. The source notes that the initial segment is a slightly coiled, wide tubule with tall stereocilia and few sperm, the caput has a narrow lumen, and lumen diameter and sperm number increase towards the corpus and cauda. Students should compare the four sections to see the lumen widen and fill with sperm along the duct.
images.author: Zhou W.; De Iuliis GN.; Dun MD.; Nixon B.
images.source_description:
Figura 1. Estructura regionalizada y distribución esquemática de los principales tipos de células en el epidídimo de ratón.

(A, B) El epidídimo del ratón generalmente se divide en cuatro segmentos anatómicos únicos: el segmento inicial, el epidídimo caput, corpus y cauda.

El segmento inicial es un túbulo ligeramente enrollado con un diámetro amplio y una baja concentración de espermatozoides. Las células epiteliales de este segmento están alargadas y poseen altos estereocilios.

El segmento de la cabeza se caracteriza por un diámetro luminal estrecho, mientras que tanto el diámetro luminal como la concentración de espermatozoides aumentan distalmente dentro del cuerpo y la cola del epidídimo.


Los diferentes tipos de células dentro de estos segmentos son responsables de la creación de un microambiente luminal especializado que promueve la maduración secuencial de los espermatozoides (capa y cuerpo del epidídimo) y su posterior almacenamiento (cola del epidídimo).

tissues.name: Ductus deferens
tissues.summary: The ductus (vas) deferens is a muscular duct that carries sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct, moving them along by peristaltic contraction of its thick smooth muscle wall. Its narrow lumen is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia, and the wall is much thicker than the lumen.
features: Narrow, irregular lumen with folded mucosa, small compared with the wall
Very thick smooth muscle wall in three layers: inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia lining the lumen
Loose adventitia outside the muscle wall, with small vessels and nerves

images.title: Vas deferens in cross-section at low power: thick muscle wall, small lumen
images.description: Low-power H&E cross-section of an unremarkable vas deferens; the source gives no magnification. The thick smooth muscle wall fills almost the whole profile around a small, irregular lumen with folded mucosa at the centre. Students should note how small the lumen is compared with the muscle, and the thin loose connective tissue at the outer edge.

tissues.name: Seminal vesicle
tissues.summary: The seminal vesicles are a pair of highly coiled glands lying behind the bladder. Their folded, secretory lining produces a fructose-rich, alkaline fluid that makes up most of the ejaculate volume.
features: Highly coiled, branching mucosal folds giving a honeycomb or labyrinthine pattern
Pseudostratified or cuboidal lining epithelium, often with yellow-brown lipofuscin pigment
Lumen filled with pale or eosinophilic secretion between the folds
Thick smooth-muscle wall around the folded mucosa
Loose connective tissue between lobules, with small blood vessels

images.title: Seminal vesicle at low power, several lobules with branching folds
images.description: Microscope field at 4x, as given in the source, showing several seminal vesicle lobules cut in section, each made of a labyrinth of branching mucosal folds around pale lumens. The stain appears to be H&E, with purple epithelium and a thick pink muscular wall around each lobule. Students should find the branching folds, the lumen between them, and the blood vessels in the connective tissue between lobules.
images.author: Luxs96
images.source_description: This microscopic image of the seminal vesicles well shows their typical labirintic appearance; it is made up of anastomosed tubules that have a cubic epithelium.

images.title: Single seminal vesicle lobule with branching mucosal folds

The source gives no magnification and describes the lining as cubic epithelium, and the stain appears to be H&E. Students should look at how the folds branch out from the central lumen, which gives the typical labyrinthine look of the gland.
images.author: Luxs96

tissues.name: Prostate
tissues.summary: The prostate is a male accessory sex gland made of branching tubuloalveolar glands set in a fibromuscular stroma that surrounds the urethra just below the bladder. Its glandular epithelium secretes a fluid that forms part of semen.
features: Papillary infoldings of the gland lining, giving folded lumens
Two cell layers: tall luminal cells over flattened basal cells
Corpora amylaceum: layered concretions in gland lumens
Fibromuscular stroma: smooth muscle and collagen between glands
Missing basal cell layer (p63-negative glands) is a key sign of carcinoma

tissues.name: Penis & erectile tissue
tissues.summary: The penis consists of three erectile bodies: the paired corpora cavernosa and the single corpus spongiosum that surrounds the urethra. Each is a mass of endothelium-lined vascular spaces enclosed by a tunica albuginea, and these spaces fill with blood to produce an erection.
features: Corpora cavernosa: endothelium-lined blood spaces (sinusoids) separated by smooth-muscle trabeculae
Corpus spongiosum: similar blood spaces packed around the urethra, which runs through its centre
Trabeculae: connective tissue with elastic fibres and bundles of smooth muscle, forming the stroma between the spaces
Tunica albuginea: a thick, dense capsule enclosing each erectile body
Helicine arteries: tightly coiled small arteries within the trabeculae that dilate during erection

tissues.name: Mammary gland
tissues.summary: The mammary gland is a branched tubuloalveolar gland that secretes milk during lactation, organised into terminal duct lobular units within fibrous and fatty stroma. Its acini and ducts have an inner luminal epithelium and an outer myoepithelial layer, which contracts to push milk out.
features: TDLU: a terminal duct with its acini, the site of most breast cancers
Two-cell lining: luminal epithelial cells inside, myoepithelial cells outside
Loose intralobular stroma within lobules vs dense interlobular stroma between them
Pink eosinophilic secretion in the acinar lumen
Lactation: distended alveoli filled with lipid-rich secretion and hobnail epithelium

tissues.name: Ovary
tissues.summary: The ovary is the female gonad, producing oocytes and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone. Its cortex holds follicles at every stage of development around a vascular medulla, and each ovulation leaves a corpus luteum that later regresses to a corpus albicans scar.
features: Surface germinal epithelium: a single layer of cells over a dense tunica albuginea
Follicles at every stage: primordial, primary, secondary and Graafian (antral)
Theca interna makes androgens; granulosa cells convert them to oestrogen
Corpus luteum after ovulation, later replaced by a pale corpus albicans scar
Vascular medulla: loose stroma packed with blood vessels at the centre

tissues.name: Uterine tube
tissues.summary: The uterine tube (fallopian tube) is a paired muscular tube that carries the oocyte from the ovary to the uterus, and the ampulla is the usual site of fertilisation. Its mucosa forms highly branched folds lined by ciliated and secretory peg cells, surrounded by inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle.
features: Highly branched mucosal folds that project into the lumen, most elaborate in the ampulla
Tall columnar epithelium with apical cilia, which beat to move the oocyte
Non-ciliated secretory peg cells between the ciliated cells, which nourish the oocyte
Thick muscular wall of inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle

tissues.name: Uterus (endometrium & myometrium)
tissues.summary: The endometrium is the mucosal lining of the uterus, made of simple columnar epithelium, tubular glands and a cellular stroma that sits on a thick smooth-muscle myometrium. Its functional layer is shed at menstruation and regenerated each cycle, and in the secretory phase it is prepared for embryo implantation.
features: Simple columnar surface epithelium lining the uterine cavity
Tubular glands in a cellular stroma; narrow and straight in the proliferative phase
Secretory phase: dilated, coiled glands with secretion in their lumens
Decidualised fibroblasts with abundant pale cytoplasm near spiral arterioles
Immune cells, likely macrophages and uterine NK cells, in the functional layer
Thick myometrium of interlacing smooth muscle beneath the endometrium

tissues.name: Cervix
tissues.summary: The cervix is the narrow, lower part of the uterus that forms a canal between the uterine cavity and the vagina. Its endocervix is lined by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium, while the ectocervix facing the vagina is covered by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, and the two meet at the transformation zone.
features: Endocervix: simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium lining branching glands and clefts
Ectocervix: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, with nuclei still present in the superficial cells
Transformation zone: the junction where squamous and columnar epithelium meet, the site where HPV-related dysplasia arises
Nabothian cysts: mucus-filled spaces where an obstructed endocervical gland has dilated

tissues.name: Vagina
tissues.summary: The vagina is a muscular, glandless canal lined by thick, non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium that is rich in glycogen. It receives the penis during intercourse and forms the lower part of the birth canal, and its moisture comes from cervical mucus and fluid that seeps through the wall rather than from glands.
features: Thick non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium whose surface cells keep their nuclei
Pale, glycogen-filled cytoplasm in the intermediate cells (glycogen shows with PAS stain)
Epithelium folded into ridges (rugae), with lamina propria filling each fold
Lamina propria rich in elastic fibres and thin-walled veins
No glands in the wall; a thick smooth muscle layer lies beneath the lamina propria

images.title: Vaginal wall: folded stratified squamous epithelium over lamina propria

A dark instrument enters from the left, but the layered epithelium and the thin-walled vessels in the lamina propria are still clear.

tissues.name: Placenta
tissues.summary: The placenta is the fetomaternal organ in which fetal chorionic villi project into maternal blood in the intervillous space, allowing exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes. The villi are covered by syncytiotrophoblast, which secretes hCG and separates fetal capillaries from maternal blood.
features: Villi covered by syncytiotrophoblast (secretes hCG) over a layer of cytotrophoblast
Cytotrophoblast layer becomes discontinuous in later pregnancy
Fetal capillaries packed with red cells in the villous stroma
Hofbauer cells (fetal macrophages) in the villous core
Decidual cells on the maternal side, in the basal plate

images.author: Silini AR, Di Pietro R, Lang-Olip I, Alviano F, Banerjee A, Basile M, Borutinskaite V, Eissner G, Gellhaus A, Giebel B, Huang Y-C, Janev A, Kreft ME, Kupper N, Abadía-Molina AC, Olivares EG, Pandolfi
images.source_title: Schematic representation of a human placenta at term
images.source_description: Figure 4. Schematic representation of a human placenta at term. The amniotic membrane is the layer closest to the fetus and is attached to the chorionic plate mesenchyme from which large stem villi reach into the intervillous space. The villous trees are fully differentiated and have a large number of terminal villi where enlarged capillaries, sinusoids, allow a higher exchange rate between maternal and fetal blood. Anchoring villi are still connected to the uterine wall, while trophoblast cell columns are exhausted. Spiral arteries invaded by endoarterial trophoblast and uterine veins invaded by endovenous trophoblast can still be found in the placental bed allowing the constant flow of maternal blood into the placenta and the drainage back into the maternal circulation (red arrows in artery and vein). Histological images of (A) term amniotic membrane with epithelium and avascular mesenchyme, (B) term chorionic plate covered by the amniotic membrane, (C) placental villi of a term placenta with a sinusoid in a terminal villus and a neighboring mature intermediate villus, (D) anchoring villus that is attached to the uterine wall where interstitial trophoblast can be found, (E) vessel in the basal plate of a term placenta. The vessel is surrounded by interstitial trophoblast. A, uterine spiral artery; AM, amniotic membrane; AV, anchoring villus; CP, chorionic plate; GA, gestational age; IT, interstitial trophoblast; MIV, mature intermediate villus; SI, sinusoid; STB, syncytiotr

tissues.name: Cornea
tissues.summary: The cornea is the transparent, avascular front of the eye, and it provides most of the eye's focusing power. It is a non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium over a stroma of regularly stacked collagen lamellae, with Bowman layer above and Descemet membrane and a single-layer endothelium below.
features: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium on the surface, with no keratin layer
Bowman layer: a thin acellular band just beneath the epithelium
Stroma: broad layer of regular collagen lamellae with flattened keratocyte nuclei between them
Descemet membrane: a sharply outlined basement membrane behind the stroma
Single endothelial layer behind Descemet membrane: does not regenerate, so losing cells causes oedema

tissues.name: Retina
tissues.summary: The retina is the thin, layered neural tissue lining the back of the eye, where photoreceptors convert light into electrical signals. Those signals pass through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons leave the eye as the optic nerve.
features: Pigment epithelium: dark brown-black layer at the outer edge, behind the photoreceptors
Photoreceptor layer: pink striped band of rod and cone outer segments
Outer nuclear layer: dense band of dark rod and cone nuclei
Inner nuclear layer: dark nuclei of bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells
Ganglion cell layer: large pale nuclei, with nerve fibres running to the optic disc
Fovea: cones only, with the inner layers pushed aside

The dark rounded profiles are most likely cell nuclei, and the brighter bands between them are probably the plexiform layers, so the image shows the layered arrangement rather than individual cell types. Students should look for the rows of dark nuclei that form the retina's nuclear layers, separated by brighter bands.

A student can follow the connections from the rods and cones down through the bipolar cells to the ganglion cells.

images.title: Rod photoreceptor structure and the layers of the retina
images.description: Multi-panel teaching figure with a toluidine blue vertical section of the retina (panel A), a schematic of a rod (panel B) and electron micrographs of its connecting cilium, outer segment discs, pigment epithelium and synaptic ribbon (panels C to H). Some labels are in Ukrainian, and the scale bars give the scale rather than a stated magnification. A student should trace the rod from the pigment epithelium through the outer segment, connecting cilium and inner segment to its synapse, and match each part to the layers in panel A.

images.source_title: Organization of rod photoreceptors in the mammalian retina
images.source_description: Organization of rod photoreceptors in the mammalian retina. (A) Vertical section of a vertebrate retina stained with toluidine blue. The retina contains five classes of neurons (photoreceptors, bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, ganglion cells), and is divided into three nuclear layers (outer nuclear layer (ONL), inner nuclear layer (INL), ganglion cell layer (GCL)) and two synaptic layers (outer plexiform layer (OPL), inner plexiform layer (IPL)); (B) Schematic of a vertebrate rod photoreceptor consisting of the long, light-sensitive outer segment (OS) enclosed by the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) which is connected via a small intracellular bridge, the connecting cilium (CC), to the metabolically active inner segment (IS) including the basal body complex (BBC; shaded in blue) and the apical region. The OS represents a modified primary cilium. The CC corresponds to the transition zone of a prototypic cilium with a (9 × 2 + 0) microtubule array; (C–H) Transmission electron micrograph of a photoreceptor-connecting cilium; (C) The CC connects the OS and IS. The BBC consists of the basal body (BB) and its centriole (Ce); (D) Cross-section of the CC showing the characteristic (9 × 2 + 0) microtubule array; (E) RPE with pigment granules and the Bruch’s membrane (BM); (F) OS composed of stacks of tightly packed membrane discs; (G) Higher magnification view of the ciliary apparatus; (H) Synaptic ribbon (SR) with invaginations of postsynaptic horizontal cells (HC) an

images.description: Fluorescence micrograph of mammalian retina in which a retinal ganglion cell is labelled green, with its branching dendrites spreading across the field. Ganglion cells are the retina's output to the brain, and a student should look for the bright green cell body and its branches set among the red amacrine cell bodies.
images.author: Jan Homann
images.source_description: Das Bild zeigt zwei verschiedene Typen von Retina Ganglienzellen, Ganglienzellen bilden den Output der Retina zum Gehirn. Diese Zellen kodieren, basierend auf dem Input der darüberliegenden Nervenzellschichten in der Retina (zum Beispiel den hier rot eingefärbten Starburst-Amakrinzellen, verschiedene Aspekte der visuellen Welt. Die Zelle mit den dünneren Dendriten zum Beispiel kodiert (mithilfe des darüber liegenden Netzwerkes von Starburst Amakrinzellen, Bipolaren Zellen und Horizontalen Zellen und Photorezeptoren), die Bewegungsrichtung von Objektion, die auf die Retina projiziert werden. Diese Information wird dann vom Gehirn genutzt, um zum Beispiel das Auge zu stabilisieren.

images.title: Nine types of retinal ganglion cell labelled with GFP
images.description: Research figure showing GFP-labelled retinal ganglion cells from rd1 retinas at 18 months of age, with nine cell types in separate panels. Each panel shows a cell body with a branching dendritic tree, its dendritic diameter and percentage stratification, and an arrow marking the axon of the representative cell. images.source_title: A large-scale survey of RGCs in rd1 retinas of 18 month-old
images.source_description:
Figure 3. A large-scale survey of RGCs in rd1 retinas of 18 month-old.

Individual RGCs are visualized by GFP expression. Representations of nine types of RGCs are shown together with their dendritic diameters and stratification in the IPL. Numbers in parentheses correspond to the cell types distinguished by Sun et al. (2002). Insets show the dendritic stratification of RGCs in the IPL. In the inset, green circle shows the location of soma, and green line indicates dendrites. The dendrites of Off and On RGCs stratified in the proximal (0–40%) and distal (40–100%) parts of the IPL, respectively. Note that this representation shows the depth of the processes only and does not attempt to show their spread. Arrows indicate axons of individual representative RGCs. INL, inner nuclear layer; IPL, inner plexiform layer; GCL, ganglion cell layer. Scale bars, 50 µm.

(A) Tulip query bundled dendrogram plot of all the sources and targets of amacrine cell 598: GC yellow circles, ganglion cells: GAC green dots, glycinergic amacrine cells; γAC red dots, GABAerigc amacrine cells; CBb cyan dots, ON cone bipolar cells; RB magenta dot, rod bipolar cell. Line color denotes the presynaptic source. Arrows denote presynaptic source in γAC to γAC paths. Each line represents a bundle of synaptic lines. (B) Validation of GABAergic identity for AC 598. (C) A gap junction between AC 598 (red) and GC 606 (yellow) delimited by arrowheads. (D) Synapse from AC 598 (red) to GC 38810 (arrow).

images.description: Black-and-white traced reconstructions (A to D) and green confocal images (E to G) of recorded retinal ganglion cells, with types labelled A, B, C, D, ON, OFF and ON-OFF. Recorded cells are filled green with Alexa 488, other cells in the ganglion cell and inner nuclear layers are red from propidium iodide, and the scale bars are 100 µm. images.author: Hadjinicolaou AE, Cloherty SL, Hung Y-S, Kameneva T, Ibbotson MR
images.source_description: Fig 1. Reconstruction of recorded cell morphology. Representative confocal image stacks typical of those used for classification of recorded retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) according to their morphological cell type. Examples are shown for representative (A) A-type, (B) B-type, (C) C-type, (D) D-type, (E) ON [C2i], (F) OFF [A2o], and (G) ON-OFF [D2] RGCs. Panels (E–G) show the en face representation (top), revealing the scale and extent of the dendritic arborisation, and a cross-section (bottom), revealing where the dendrites of each cell stratify within the inner plexiform layer (IPL). Long-dashed lines indicate the boundary of the IPL and short-dashed lines indicate the approximate boundary between the two sublaminae. Recorded cells were labelled, via the patch pipette, with Alexa488 (green). Other cells in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) and inner nuclear layer (INL) were labelled with propidium iodide (red).

images.title: Wiring diagram of the AII amacrine cell network in the retina
images.description: A wiring diagram, not a microscope image, of the AII amacrine cell network in the retina, showing glutamate, dopamine, GABA, glycine and peptide inputs and outputs to OFF bipolar cells and two classes of OFF ganglion cells. The image belongs to the retina tissue, since the layers shown (photoreceptors to ganglion cell layer) are retinal.
images.author: Marc RE, Anderson JR, Jones BW, Sigulinsky CL and Lauritzen JS
images.source_title: The new AII amacrine cell network
images.source_description: Figure 14. The new AII amacrine cell network. The complete AII cell network spans 4 classes of excitatory glutamate inputs, three coupling partners, dopamine modulation, three wide-field GABAergic inputs, peptide modulation, narrow-field glycinergic input, and outputs to OFF bipolar cells, OFF inhibitory neurons and two classes of OFF ganglion cells. All classes of CBb (except CBb7) and CBa bipolar cells are lumped into single ON and OFF channels. Multiple classes of ON and OFF amacrine cells are lumped into single representative classes. Dashed lines show paths for cone → rod suppressive crossover. TH1 AxC is a dual glutamate/dopamine wide-field axonal cell. PRL, photoreceptor layer; OPL, outer plexiform layer; INL, inner nuclear layer; IPL, inner plexiform layer; GCL, ganglion cell layer. Icon key at bottom denotes connection types. The OFF band captures the AII neck and lobules, which do not overlap with neighboring AII cells. The ON band captures the waist and the heavily coupled arboreal network, which overlaps other AII cells with a coverage factor of 4. Colored dots denote postsynaptic sites for each modality.

tissues.name: Eyeball, lens & eyelid
tissues.summary: The walls and lens of the eyeball, together with the eyelids: a fibrous sclera continuous with the cornea, the pigmented uvea (iris, ciliary body and choroid), the transparent lens and the protective eyelids. The ciliary body secretes aqueous humour, and the lens helps focus light onto the retina.
features: Sclera: dense irregular collagenous connective tissue, continuous with the transparent cornea
Ciliary body: ciliary muscle and ciliary processes that secrete aqueous humour
Iris: pigmented stroma with sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles
Lens: thick capsule, a single layer of anterior cuboidal epithelium and anucleate lens fibres
Eyelid: tarsal plate with meibomian glands, orbicularis oculi and conjunctiva with goblet cells

images.title: Lens schematic: anterior epithelium, lens fibres and nucleus

Look for the central lens nucleus with radiating sutures and the fibres that fill most of the lens.

tissues.name: Inner ear & cochlea
tissues.summary: The membranous labyrinth of the inner ear houses the sensory organs of hearing and balance. Hair cells in the cochlear duct and in the utricle, saccule and semicircular ducts convert sound and head movement into nerve signals.
features: Cochlear duct lying between scala vestibuli and scala tympani
Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane under the tectorial membrane
One row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells in the organ of Corti
Stria vascularis on the outer wall of the duct, secreting potassium-rich endolymph
Maculae with otoliths (utricle, saccule); cristae ampullares in the semicircular ducts
Gaps in the hair cell rows after aminoglycoside or noise damage, with outer hair cells usually lost first

images.title: Cochlea overview with organ of Corti and hair cell bundles (diagram)
images.description: A composite teaching figure: a schematic of the cochlea, a cross-section of the organ of Corti with inner and outer hair cells under the tectorial membrane, and scanning electron micrographs of hair cell bundles from the base and apex. The basal bundle (high-frequency) has shorter stereocilia than the apical bundle (low-frequency), so students should link stereocilia length to position along the cochlea. The electron micrographs are not stained sections, so no stain applies.
images.author: Kassim YM, Rosenberg DB, Das S, Wang X, Huang Z, Rahman S, et al.
images.source_description:
Fig 1. The anatomy of the cochlea [35].

Sensory hair cell stereocilia sit along a tonotopic axis that follows the length of the spiral-shaped cochlea with a striking pattern of increasing stereocilia lengths from the base to the apex of the cochlea. The morphological and spatial features of cochlear hair cell stereocilia follow extremely predictable tonotopic patterns between individuals and species: Stereocilia lengths increase as a function of position along the tonotopic axis of the cochlea, which in turn is reflective of the frequency of sound they are tuned to detect. Thus, the relationship between the morphological and spatial features of these cells and their function are relatively well-defined compared to many other biological systems. Due to their highly patterned organization, cochlear tissues thus present a particularly striking opportunity for automated computer vision tasks.

images.title: Organ of Corti in cross-section and outer hair cell movement
images.description: Four panels on the organ of Corti: a schematic cross-section (A), an in vivo optical coherence tomography image of the living organ (B), and cartoons of outer hair cells at rest (C) and contracting when depolarised (D). No stain applies, as these are diagrams and an imaging scan rather than a stained section. Students should learn the layers (tectorial membrane, reticular lamina, basilar membrane) and the positions of the inner and outer hair cells, not cell detail.
images.author: Zha D, Chen F, Ramamoorthy S, Fridberger A, Choudhury N, Jacques SL, et al.
images.source_description:
Figure 1. The cochlea structure and function.

a. The illustrated organ of Corti in cross-section. b. An OCT image of the organ of Corti in vivo. Circles mark the locations of vibration measurement. c. A cartoon of hair cell excitation without OHC length change. d. A cartoon showing that when depolarized, OHCs contract to become shorter in length. This will draw together the reticular lamina and basilar membrane; IHC, inner hair cell; OHC, outer hair cell; PCs, pillar cells.

images.title: Cochlear and vestibular hair cells with their nerve endings (diagram)
images.description: A diagram comparing hair cells: on the left, cochlear inner and outer hair cells with their stereocilia, ribbon synapses, afferent and efferent nerve endings and Schwann cells; on the right, type I and type II vestibular hair cells, with the calyx wrapped around the type I cell. Students should note the calyx, the kinocilium and the afferent and efferent endings, which help tell the cell types apart. No stain applies, as this is a diagram.
images.author: Masetto S, Spaiardi P, J. Johnson S.
images.source_title: Auditory and vestibular hair cells and their innervation in adult mammals
images.source_description: Figure 2. Auditory and vestibular hair cells and their innervation in adult mammals. Left: in the cochlea, Bouton afferent nerve terminals (red) occur at the basolateral membrane and face a single ellipsoid synaptic body (ribbon, large yellow oval) per active zone in both IHCs and OHCs – Some terminals are not shown in figure for clarity. Presynaptic vesicles (yellow filled circles) containing the afferent neurotransmitter (glutamate) are shown tethered to the ribbon. Voltage-gated CaV1.3 Ca2+ channels (green) are clustered at the presynaptic membrane, opposed to glutamatergic AMPA receptors (magenta) at the afferent postsynaptic membrane. The zoom shows a presynaptic zone facing the postsynaptic membrane. IHCs only form afferent synapses (5 to 30) with type I (myelinated) spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), which represent ~95% of all SGNs. OHCs form afferent synapses with the remaining ~5% type II (unmyelinated) SGNs. Each type I SGN only forms a single synaptic contact with a single IHC. By contrast, each type II SGN contacts several OHCs. Efferent Bouton nerve terminals (blue) synapse onto type I SGN boutons in close proximity to IHCs (unmyelinated lateral olivocochlear (LOC) neurons), or directly contact OHCs (myelinated medial olivocochlear (MOC) neurons). Only a single LOC efferent is shown for clarity while, in reality, a rich plexus of endings is formed beneath each IHC. Presynaptic vesicles (green filled circles) containing the efferent neurotransmitter (acetylcholine)

images.title: Gentamicin hair cell loss in a cochlear explant (fluorescence)
images.description: Fluorescence confocal micrographs of a stage P2 cochlear explant, with hair cell nuclei in green (Atoh1/nGFP) and hair cell bodies in red (myosin VI antibody). Panels B to M show the outer (ohc) and inner (ihc) hair cell rows 24 hours after gentamicin at 0, 10, 50 and 100 µg/ml, and the bar graph (N) shows hair cell counts falling sharply at 50 and 100 µg/ml. Scale bars are 100 µm (A) and 50 µm (B to M); students should look for gaps in the hair cell rows and the white arrows marking debris.
images.author: Korrapati S, Roux I, Glowatzki E, Doetzlhofer A
images.source_title: Gentamicin exposure results in rapid inner and outer hair cell loss
images.source_description:
Figure 1. Gentamicin exposure results in rapid inner and outer hair cell loss.

A: Acutely isolated cochlear explant (stage P2). Atoh1/nGFP expression (green) labels inner and outer hair cell nuclei. Red lines subdivide auditory sensory epithelium into apex, mid apex, mid base and base. Scale bar 100 μm. B–M: Hair cell phenotype 24 hours after exposure to various concentrations of gentamicin. Confocal images are taken from the central part of mid apical segment (A, white box). Brackets mark outer hair cell domain (ohc), arrowheads point to inner hair cell domain (ihc). Myosin VI antibody staining (Myo6, red) labels cytoplasmic domain of hair cells. Atoh1/nGFP transgene (green) labels hair cell nuclei. Scale bar 50 μm. B–D: control (0 μg/ml gentamicin). E–G: 10 μg/ml gentamicin. H–J: 50 μg/ml gentamicin. White arrow marks Myo6 positive hair cell debris. K–M: 100 μg/ml gentamicin. N: Quantification of B-M. Hair cell numbers were analyzed in the mid apical segment. Data expressed as mean ±SEM (n = 3 cochlear explants from 2 independent experiments; ** p≤0.0001, Student's t-test; p>0.05 was considered not significant (n.s.)).

images.title: Organ of Corti in cross-section during activation (schematic)
images.description: A simplified schematic of the organ of Corti in cross-section, with three hair cells on the left and one curved cell on the right in pink, beneath the tectorial membrane (dark blue) and above red nerve fibres. The inset at top left shows the stereocilia tilting when the hair cells are activated. It is stylised and unstained, so use it to learn the layout rather than exact cell shape.

images.source_description: The organ of Corti being activated.

images.title: Cochlear nerve supply: spiral ganglion neurons and hair cell connections
images.description: A diagram plus immunofluorescence panels from a mouse cochlea showing how spiral ganglion neurons link the hair cells to the brainstem. Whole-mount panels show outer hair cells labelled for prestin (green), inner hair cells labelled for calretinin (red), and spiral ganglion neuron cell bodies labelled for NeuN (red) with nerve fibres labelled for tubulin; scale bars are 50 µm. Panel D shows the three types of type I afferent terminal (Ia, Ib, Ic) on one inner hair cell.
images.author: Pavlinkova, G.
images.source_title: Auditory neurons form the spiral ganglion in the cochlea and connect hair cells in the organ of Corti to cochlear nuclei in the brain stem
images.source_description:
Figure 1. Auditory neurons form the spiral ganglion in the cochlea and connect hair cells in the organ of Corti to cochlear

nuclei in the brain stem. (A) Diagram shows innervation of the organ of Corti. Type I neurons extend radial ﬁbers toward the inner hair cells (5–30 type I neurons innervate one inner hair cell), and type II neurons provide diffuse innervations to the outer hair cells and supporting cells within the cochlea. Efferent axons from superior olivary complex innervate the outer hair cells. (B) Whole-mount immunolabeling of the mouse cochlea shows outer hair cells (OHC, labeled by anti-prestin) and inner hair cells (IHC, labeled by anti-calretinin) forming the organ of Corti (OC). (C) Whole-mount immunostaining of the spiral ganglion (SG) neurons (anti-NeuN, a neuronal soma marker) shows the dendrites extending in the periphery to the organ of Corti (OC) and the axons traveling to the central nervous system (anti-acetylated alpha-tubulin-labeled nerve ﬁbers). Scale bars, 50 µm. Confocal images (B) taken from [6] and (C) unpublished data. (D) Schematic drawing of synapses of molecular subtypes of type I neurons on the inner hair cell. Type I neurons are segregated into three distinct groups: types Ia (blue), Ib (magenta), and Ic (green-blue) of the spiral auditory neurons, which extend peripheral processes that are spatially segregated on the surface of the IHC. HS: Hoechst nuclear staining.

tissues.name: Spinal cord
tissues.summary: The spinal cord is the part of the central nervous system inside the vertebral canal, carrying ascending and descending nerve tracts and housing motor neurons and reflex circuits. In cross-section, grey matter forms an H-shaped core around the central canal, surrounded by white matter tracts.
features: Anterior horns: large multipolar motor neurons with Nissl bodies in their cytoplasm
Posterior horns: the sensory input region; the substantia gelatinosa at the tip processes pain
Lateral horns (T1 to L2): preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Central canal at the centre of the grey matter, lined by ependyma
White matter tracts outside the grey matter; myelinated fibres stain blue with luxol fast blue

A student should find the H-shaped grey matter around the central canal and the white matter outside it.

tissues.name: Cerebral cortex
tissues.summary: The cerebral cortex is the thin outer layer of grey matter covering the cerebral hemispheres, where sensory information is processed, voluntary movement is planned and higher mental functions take place. Most of it is six-layered neocortex, with pyramidal and granular neurons arranged in layers and supported by glia.
features: Six layers, I (molecular) to VI (multiform), with the cell types changing from layer to layer
Layer I is cell-poor, with mostly fibres and few cell bodies
Layers II and IV are packed with small granular neurons; layers III and V hold pyramidal neurons, the largest in layer V
Layer V of the primary motor cortex contains giant Betz cells
Primary visual cortex has a thick layer IV with the stria of Gennari, a band of myelinated fibres
Glia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia) are scattered through the neuropil, seen as small dark nuclei

tissues.name: Cerebellum
tissues.summary: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and motor learning, and its cortex is a tightly folded sheet of grey matter with three layers around white-matter cores called arbor vitae. Its only output is the Purkinje cell layer, which sends inhibitory (GABA) signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei.
features: Molecular layer: the outer, pale, sparsely populated layer with few stellate and basket cell nuclei
Purkinje cell layer: a single row of large flask-shaped neurons at the boundary between the molecular and granular layers
Granular layer: densely packed small dark granule cell nuclei, the most cellular layer of the cortex
Arbor vitae: the pale white-matter core of each folium
Deep nuclei such as the dentate: larger, scattered neurons among fibres in the white matter

tissues.name: Hippocampus
tissues.summary: The hippocampus proper is a three-layered archicortex in the medial temporal lobe that is essential for forming new declarative memories. Its principal cells are the CA pyramidal neurons and dentate granule cells, and CA1 is especially vulnerable to hypoxia.
features: CA1 (Sommer sector): a dense band of pyramidal neurons lying next to the subiculum
CA fields: pyramidal cell layer with stratum oriens on one side and stratum radiatum on the other
Dentate gyrus granule cell layer: a tightly packed, V- or U-shaped band of small round neurons
Hilus: scattered larger neurons inside the fold of the granule cell layer
Molecular layer: cell-poor neuropil outside the granule cells, towards the hippocampal fissure
Alveus and fimbria: white fibre tracts running over the surface of the CA fields

images.title: Reconstructed pyramidal and granule neurons on a hippocampal outline
images.description: A drawn diagram rather than a micrograph, with black neuron reconstructions and dendritic trees placed along a beige hippocampal outline. The source describes it as Figure 8C of a study on neuronal branching, in which granule cells were positioned along a dentate gyrus contour traced from a sketch by Camillo Golgi. It shows the general arrangement of pyramidal and granule cells and the direction of their dendrites, which is useful for orientation but is not a stained section.

images.title: Marmoset hippocampal subdivisions: stained sections and schematics

images.source_title: Hippocpus-Principal hippocampal subdivisions in the marmoset
images.source_description:
Principal hippocampal subdivisions in the marmoset (Callithrix jacchus). (A) Major hippocampal subdivisions in Giemsa-stained marmoset mid-septotemporal hippocampus. Arrows mark the boundaries between subdivisions at the level of the cell layer(s). (B) Definitions of the principal cell population in the marmoset mid-septotemporal hippocampus. (C) Complex hilar cytoarchitecture of the marmoset dentate gyrus that is common in non-rodent species. (D) Definitions of the regions that have been used to define CA3 and hilar cell populations within the dentate gyrus; 1: CA3 or CA3o (outer CA3, Houser et al., 1990), 2: reflected blade of CA3 (Lorente De Nó, 1934) or CA3h (used in this study; Lim et al., 1997; Ding and Van Hoesen, 2015) or CA3i (inner CA3, Houser et al., 1990) or CA4 (Rosene and Van Hoesen, 1987), 3: polymorphic cell layer (2+3: CA4 of Lorente De Nó, 1934), and 4: plexiform layer (Cajal, 1968), 5: dentate granule cells. Stratum radiatum (6) and stratum oriens (7) insert themselves superficial and deep to CA3h. The separation between CA3h and the hilar polymorphic layer is variable in different species and at different septotemporal levels. When the CA3h and the polymorphic cell layer merge, we cannot reliably distinguish CA3h cells from hilar polymorphic cells in Nissl-stained preparations. Scale bars: 250 μm.
From: Front. Neuroanat., 09 March 2016 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fnana.2016.00022

tissues.name: Brainstem & basal ganglia
tissues.summary: The brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla) contains cranial nerve nuclei and pigmented nuclei such as the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus, threaded with myelinated tracts. The basal ganglia, including the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), are deep grey matter nuclei that help control movement.
features: Neuromelanin: brown granular cytoplasm in substantia nigra and locus coeruleus neurons
Pontine nuclei: granular neuropil of small neurons, divided by blue myelinated fibre bundles
Cranial nerve motor nuclei: clusters of large multipolar neurons beside the fourth ventricle
Striatum (caudate and putamen): pink neuropil crossed by myelinated fibre bundles
Locus coeruleus: pigmented neurons in the lateral floor of the fourth ventricle

tissues.name: Meninges & choroid plexus
tissues.summary: The meninges are three connective tissue layers (dura, arachnoid and pia mater) that enclose the brain and spinal cord. The choroid plexus is a highly vascular structure projecting into the brain ventricles that secretes cerebrospinal fluid, and its epithelial cells are joined by tight junctions that form the blood-CSF barrier.
features: Dura: dense, collagen-rich fibrous connective tissue forming the outer layer
Arachnoid: thin sheet with delicate trabeculae crossing the subarachnoid space
Pia: thin layer adhering closely to the surface of the brain or spinal cord
Choroid plexus: fronds of fenestrated capillaries covered by cuboidal epithelium with microvilli
Choroid plexus epithelial cells joined by tight junctions, forming the blood-CSF barrier
Arachnoid cap cells, the origin of meningiomas, which may contain psammoma bodies

images.title: Blood-brain and blood-CSF barriers, including the choroid plexus
images.description: Labelled schematic (not a microscope image) of the brain showing four barrier sites: the blood-brain barrier in cerebral vessels, the blood-CSF barrier of the choroid plexus, the pia arachnoid barrier and the CSF-brain barrier of the ventricle lining, which is only present in development. The choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles is shown in red, and its inset shows fenestrated plexus capillaries, epithelial cells joined by tight junctions and epiplexus immune cells on the CSF side. Students should be able to say which cells and junctions form each barrier.
images.author: Stolp HB, Liddelow SA, Sá-Pereira I, Dziegielewska KM and Saunders NR
images.source_description: Protective barriers of the brain. The collective term “blood-brain barrier” is used to describe four main interfaces between the central nervous system and the periphery. (i) The blood-brain barrier proper formed by tight junctions between the endothelial cells of the cerebral vasculature. It is thought that pericytes (peri.) are sufficient to induce some barrier characteristics in endothelial cells, while astrocytes (astro.) are able to maintain the integrity of the blood-brain barrier postnatally. (ii) The blood-CSF barrier formed by tight junctions between epithelial cells of the choroid plexus epithelial cells (note the plexus vasculature is fenestrated). Resident epiplexus (epi.) immune cells are present on the CSF-surface of the plexus epithelium. (iii) The outer CSF-brain barrier and the level of the pia arachnoid, formed by tight junctions between endothelial cells of the arachnoid vessels. (iv) The inner CSF-brain barrier, present only in early development, formed by strap junctions between the neuroependymal cells lining the ventricular surfaces. In the adult this barrier is no longer present. Both the blood-brain and CSF-brain barriers extend down the spinal cord. The CSF-filled ventricular system is depicted in blue, while CNS brain tissue is in brown. The lateral ventricular choroid plexuses are shown in red. Abbreviations: astro, astrocyte; bv, blood vessel; cpec, choroid plexus epithelial cell; csf, cerebrospinal fluid; peri, pericytes.
